Social media platforms, such as Twitter, have become an essential source of data for researchers and practitioners who aim to understand the behavior, sentiment, and emotions of large populations. The ever-growing availability of social media data has led to a surge in the development of various models for predicting community-level outcomes based on the aggregated text from social media posts. Nowcasting, in particular, has gained significant attention due to its ability to provide unobtrusive and near real-time predictions of potential outcomes. A common approach to nowcasting relies on aggregating all social media posts without consideration for individual users, which assumes that aggregated data reflects the collective behavior of the community. However, research has shown that aggregating data without regard to users may lead to inaccurate or biased estimates of the population's behavior, attitudes, and emotions. Consequently, an increasing number of researchers and practitioners have started to explore alternative approaches to nowcasting that focus on individual users and their social connections. This shift towards user-level analysis is driven by the understanding that each user contributes distinctly to the aggregated data, which can lead to improved accuracy and reduced bias in predictions. By examining the language aggregated by user, researchers can identify patterns, trends, and relevant correlations that may be hidden when analyzing aggregated data. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective method for building community-level models using Twitter language aggregated by user. We demonstrate the benefits of this approach through results on four different U.S. county-level tasks, spanning demographic, health, and psychological outcomes. Our experiments show large and consistent improvements in prediction accuracies over the standard approach of aggregating all tweets. For instance, in terms of median income prediction, our results show a significant increase from a Pearson r value of 0.73 to 0.82. Similarly, for life satisfaction prediction, our approach leads to an improvement from a Pearson r value of 0.37 to 0.47. Our research contributes to the growing body of literature that highlights the importance of considering individual users in social media analysis. By leveraging user-level data, we can gain deeper insights into the collective behavior of social media users, ultimately leading to more accurate predictions of community-level outcomes. To facilitate further research, we provide access to our aggregated and anonymized community-level data, derived from 37 billion tweets, with over 1 billion of which were mapped to counties.

Code-switching, a phenomenon where individuals switch between two or more languages in a single conversation, is a common occurrence worldwide, especially in multicultural communities. However, code-switching poses significant challenges to natural language processing (NLP) applications, such as part-of-speech (POS) tagging, where the model struggles to identify the language of the input text. This issue is further exacerbated when the input text contains transliteration, where words from one language are represented using the script of another language (e.g., English words written in Hindi script). Despite the prevalence of code-switching, NLP models often rely on explicit language identification (ELI) to determine the language of the input text, which is not only error-prone but also requires large amounts of labeled data for different languages. In contrast, this paper proposes an innovative approach to addressing the challenges of code-switching by developing a novel model architecture that can be trained and deployed without requiring explicit language identification. Our approach, which we call "inference-driven, multi-language POS tagging," leverages the flexibility of neural network architectures to jointly maintain separate word representations for each possible language or script. This design enables our model to generalize across different languages and scripts, allowing it to make accurate POS tagging decisions without requiring explicit language identification. Our model is based on the idea of representational independence, where each language or script is treated as a separate entity with its own internal representation. This is achieved by introducing a novel module, called the "languageattention mechanism," which allows the model to dynamically attend to the relevant language or script based on the input text. By maintaining separate representations for each language or script, our model can learn to identify the language or script of the input text without requiring explicit language identification. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted experiments on Hindi-English POS tagging, a microtask of the Larger-than-S-SIZED- Switching (LTSS) dataset (jaiswal and Sauikshya Vaish 2019), which consists of code-switched Hindi-English text with alternate scripts. We trained our model on monolingual resources and tested its performance on the LTSS dataset, which includes both code-switched and monolingual text. The evaluation results show that our approach significantly outperforms standard models, including the well-known transformer architecture (Vaswani et al. 2017) that relies on explicit language identification. The contributions of this paper are threefold: (1) we introduce a novel model architecture that can be trained exclusively on monolingual resources; (2) we propose the language-attention mechanism to dynamically attend to the relevant language or script; and (3) we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on Hindi-English

Image retrieval models have been a cornerstone of computer vision research for decades, with applications ranging from content-based image retrieval to object recognition. Conventional image retrieval models represent images as a bag-of-terms, where each image is reduced to a set of visual features or descriptors, typically extracted from predefined regions or directly from the entire image. These representations are particularly well-suited for matching images based on the presence or absence of certain features. However, for certain types of queries, a more nuanced understanding of how image regions relate to each other is necessary. For instance, imagine a user searching for images of people performing specific actions, such as someone cooking in a kitchen. While a bag-of-terms representation might return images of people holding kitchen utensils, it will struggle to distinguish between images of people who are simply interacting with objects versus those who are actively engaging in the activity. Incorporating spatial information about the relationships between image regions is crucial for capturing the complexities of human activity understanding in image retrieval. Visual Dependency Representations (VDRs) aim to address this by providing a structured representation of image regions, which captures their syntactic relationships to one another. In a VDR, an image is represented as a directed graph, where nodes are image regions, and edges encode the dependency relationships between these regions. For example, in an image of a person stirring a pot, the person node might depend on the stirring motion node, which in turn depends on the pot node, and so on. This high-level representation of image structure enables distinguishing between images where objects only co-occur from images where they interact or are manipulated by the subject. In this paper, we investigate the utility of VDRs for improving image retrieval performance on query-by-example tasks, where a user provides an example image and seeks similar images in a database. Specifically, we conduct a thorough evaluation of VDRs on the Stanford-Action dataset, a benchmark collection of images depicting 8 action categories. In an end-to-end histogram comparison and query-by-example experiment, we compare the performance of VDRs against a more traditional bag-of-terms baseline. Our results demonstrate that VDRs are a viable alternative to bag-of-terms representations, yielding a 8.8% relative improvement in MAP and 8.6% relative improvement in Precision@10. Our findings provide evidence that structured representations of image regions, such as those captured by VDRs, can serve as a valuable complement to more traditional feature-based retrieval approaches.

Discourse parsing is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), aiming to hierarchically identify the discourse relations within a text and assign them to a specific scope. Among various discourse parsing frameworks, the Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST)-style document-level discourse parsing has drawn significant attention in recent years due to its ability to capture group-level relationships and use discourse relations to understand the global meaning of a text. However, RST-style document-level discourse parsing remains a challenging task, mainly due to the complex nature of discourse relations, the large number of possible discourse structures, and the need to capture the interactions between distant elements in the text. Despite the advancements in NLP, the deep learning-based approaches for RST-style document-level discourse parsing have rarely been thoroughly studied. The lack of efficient deep learning models for this task makes manual feature engineering a conventional method to achieve acceptable performance, leading to the proliferation of complex and cumbersome feature engineering pipelines. In this context, developing a deep learning model that can directly learn useful representations of discourse structures and relations from raw text data without extensive manual feature engineering is highly desirable. Towards this goal, we propose a novel attention-based hierarchical neural network (AHNN) for RST-style document-level discourse parsing. In particular, we design a tensor-based transformation function to model the complicated feature interactions, which is differentiable and can be solved via backpropagation. Our model is able to dynamically focus on relevant parts of the text and learn hierarchical representations that capture the discourse relations and their scopes. Extensive experiments on the discourse parsed data demonstrate that our approach achieves comparable or even better performance than the contemporary state-of-the-art systems with limited manual feature engineering, while significantly improving the processing efficiency. In addition, we provide an in-depth analysis of our proposed model, including itsarchitecture, the tensor-based transformation function, and the attention mechanism. Our results highlight the effectiveness of the deep learning-based approach for RST-style document-level discourse parsing and reveal an alternative to the conventional manual feature engineering methods. By leveraging the AHNN and tensor-based transformation function, we are able to directly learn from raw text data and provide interpretable internal representations that contribute to the discourse understanding. These results offer a fruitful foundation for future research on discourse parsing and related NLP applications. Our proposed model is also envisioned to be more adaptable and extendable to other NLP tasks, which require modeling complex hierarchical relationships.

The Standard Model of sequence generation in neural machine translation (NMT) consists of an autoregressive encoder-decoder architecture, where the decoder predicts the next word in the target sequence conditioned on the entire source sequence and previous target words (Sutskever et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2014). Despite the autoregressive property of these models, they are computationally expensive, especially when processing long sequences (Denkowski and Lavie, 2015; Hieber et al., 2017). With the growing demand for online translation, decoding speed has become a major concern in the field of NMT. The autoregressive decoding mechanism serializes the computation of each target word, one at a time, limiting the parallelization depth and thus preventing efficient utilization of modern multi-core processors. One potential solution to this problem is to abandon the autoregressive property, as done in non-autoregressive models (Gu et al., 2017; Gehring et al., 2017). However, these models often neglect the global context, leading to inferior translation quality (Lewis et al., 2019). In this paper, we propose a novel semi-autoregressive model, named Semi-Autoregressive Transformer (SAT), which keeps the autoregressive property in global but alleviates it in local. The SAT is designed to balance between two conflicting goals: parallelizing the decoding process while preserving translation quality. In the proposed model, the encoder generates a global context vector, which is then fed into the decoder. Instead of autoregressively predicting the next word, the decoder is allowed to generate multiple successive words in parallel at each time step. We also propose a learning algorithm to efficiently update the weights of the SAT, and demonstrate its practical effectiveness with experiments conducted on two popular translation tasks: English-German and Chinese-English. This work builds upon the well-known Transformer model (Vaswani et al., 2017) and exploits its strengths while attempting to address its main weakness-the serial decoding scheme. To validate the effectiveness of our proposed model, we compare the SAT with several state-of-the-art autoregressive and non-autoregressive baselines, including the Transformer model, the autoregressive Transformer-XL (Dai et al., 2019) and the non-autoregressive Transformer-XL variant. Our experimental results demonstrate that the SAT achieves a promising trade-off between translation quality and decoding speed on the above tasks. On WMT14 English-German translation task, the SAT achieves a 5.58 × speedup while maintaining 88% translation quality compared to the Transformer-based baseline. With more aggressive parallelization, producing two words at each time step, the SAT is almost lossless, with only a 1% degeneration in BLEU score.

Resolution of reference in natural language involves recognizing that content words such as noun phrases (NPs) can occur with different referents in multiple clauses. Consider an example like "Paul, who was very unhappy with his boss, was tired from the meeting. He went to his sister's house to collect himself, and then he proceeded to his favourite ha group with Knut and Mandy to drink tea." In this example, three pronouns (He, his, his) co-refer to three different referents (Paul, Paul, Paul). The first pronominal reference is obvious as pronouns are typically used to refer to entities that co-refer to the antecedent NP "Paul, who was very unhappy with his boss". However, later the pronoun "He" again refers to "Paul", which involves less obvious inference. We cannot come to this inference by just looking at the sentences if we ignore the content of the antecedent NP. Thus it is clear that coreference involves more complex, abstract reasoning than more traditional tasks. For a long time, machine learning approaches, which rely more on information collected in the features than perform complex semantics-level inference, have been widely relevant for various tasks, especially for tasks in natural language processing. Unfortunately, these methods find it difficult to capture certain context-variables signaled by coreferential sentences as they may overlook relationships that depend on deeper linguistic features. Inference-based methods dealing with coreference seen, in contrast, attempt to relate the task first and foremost to complex inference solutions by adding the although symbolic knowledge found in features and exploitation of large knowledge resources such as WordNet. The goal in this paper is to present a systematic investigation into how inference-based approaches might be used in dealing with problems of coreference and demonstrate the practical use of these approaches in coreference in a general formal framework in inference-based discourse processing. This work forms a significant extension of Hobbs et al. (1993)'s original-weighted abduction inference from knowledge base and weighted unification concept for reducing to the traditional, unwanted overmerging phenomenon inherent within inference approaches. Overmerging occurs when inference-based systems make the error of taking unrelated entities to be identical, which can have a severe impact on coreference. By expanding Hobbs's work to include weighted unifications that fits well with a set of relations where unification weights need to be introduced for knowledge that gets stored in the discourse theory, we describe an extended-generalized conception of abduction inference applicable to discourse processing for determining whether different entities through resolution of events via permutations of coreferential resolutions could prevent undesirable effects such as overmerging.

Natural language processing (NLP) has made tremendous strides in recent years with the advent of deep learning techniques. A key application area for NLP nowadays is digital personal assistants, such as Siri, Google Assistant, and Alexa, which rely heavily on machine understanding to execute user's commands. One of the NLP challenges facing these assistants is semantic parsing, where they need to translate natural language input into an executable representation that can be understood and acted upon by the underlying system. A fundamental component of this process is understanding rules and constraints expressed by users using natural language. The primary focus of this paper is on understanding If-Then statements, which are a common format for expressing rules. However, the techniques presented here should be portable to other semantic parsing tasks, making the work more widely applicable. The task of semantic parsing involves mapping an input sentence to a structured representation. In the context of If-Then statements, if A, B and C are the action/condition statements, then the semantic parser needs to identify the "if" condition and the consequent action "then." In terms of formal representation, the goal is to assign labels to the input sentence indicating the semantics of the If-Then statement. One common way to view this is as a structure prediction problem (Durrett and Klein, 2015), where the goal is to predict the structured output, comprised of labels and corresponding relationships. There are three key aspects to this problem: (1) parsing and semantic role labeling (SRL), (2) conditional logic, and (3) although straightforward, assignment of action and condition labels. Conventional techniques for solving this task have employed first-order logic (e.g. Propensity by Wang et al., 2007) and integer linear programming (ILP), and by Cai et al., 2013, both of which have been shown to achieve high accuracy. However, the most recent advancements indicate that deep learning models can be just as effective (Koppal et al., 2015),(Müller et al., 2016), and indeed more flexible. Furthermore, recent deep learning models also provide intuition on the contributed error type. There are two types of mistakes which can be made by the parser. Firstly, there is an incorrect prediction where the parser predicts an unrelated If-Then statement. Secondly, this involves predicting the correct "if" condition plus action, but there is a misorder of action or incorrect first condition term additions. These are referred to asparsers or position errors.

Understanding the meaning of a text cannot be reduced to simply reading the words as they appear on the page. Rather, the reader actively engages with the text, constructing a mental representation that conveys the author's intended message. This process, whereby the reader infers and elaborates upon the meaning of a text, is often referred to as an "inferential" or "constructionist" view of comprehension (Millis and Stahl, 2006). From this perspective, the goal of reading is not just to recognize individual words, but to create a rich, coherent picture of the world being described. This picture, or "scene," constitutes the reader's understanding of the text, and can be used to inform new inferences and answers to questions that go beyond the specific content of the text (Grafton, 2009). The process of constructing a scene from a text is not unique to reading comprehension, but rather is a fundamental aspect of human cognition (Meyer, 1975). When we encounter new information, whether through text, speech, or observation, we automatically begin to construct a mental representation of the scene, using our prior knowledge and experience to fill in gaps and make sense of what we encounter (Tversky, 1975). This process is especially critical for understanding certain types of texts, such as narratives, where the reader must piece together a sequence of events and characters to form a coherent picture of the story (Zwaan, 1993). In this paper, we explore the application of scene construction theory to answering elementary science questions. Specifically, we propose that, when confronted with a science text, readers construct a mental scene that represents their understanding of the text, and that this scene can be used to answer a wide range of questions that go beyond the specific content of the text. We will present a set of experiments that demonstrate the utility of this approach, and discuss the implications for teaching and learning in science education. Generating a coherent and concise summary from a long piece of text is an essential task in natural language processing, with applications in information retrieval, question answering, and text summarization. Traditional summarization methods, such as extractive and abstractive summarization, have been well-studied, but they often fail to capture the coherence of the input text (Liu et al., 2009). Most existing summarization methods aim to select the most relevant sentences from the source document and order them to form a summary. However, this process can result in a summary that is not coherent with the original document. Coherence is particularly important in summarization, as it can help readers to quickly understand the main points of the document and grasp the underlying relationships between the different ideas (Radev and McKeown, 2003). Many approaches to modeling coherence in summarization rely on the use of graph-based models, such as the Topic-Sentiment Graph (Chen et al., 2011), or on the exploitation of more structured representations of text, such as topic modeling (Mihalcea and Csomai, 2007). In the graph-based approach, sentences are integrated into a graph, and the coherence of a sentence is based on the connectivity with the previous sentences. For certain type of texts such as news articles, sentences can be connected by their similar topics, entities, or time. However, this way of deciding the coherence might not apply to all types of documents. In addition, the results of these methods are based solely on the assignment of features and weights, and the relationships between the sentences are hard to visualize and interpret. To address this challenge, a Hidden Semi-Markov Model (HSMM) has been popularized in the applications of natural language processing, such as parsing, dialogue, and sequence labeling tasks, due to its effectiveness in modeling sequential data with variable-length segments (Russell and Norvig, 2009). In this study, we propose a novel summarization method based on HSMM, which can naturally model the relationship between the sentence succession and the coherence of the summary. In our proposed method, we take advantage of the strengths of HSMM, including modeling variable-length segments, sequential dependencies, and probabilistic prediction. Our method optimizes the selection of sentences to form the summary with the objective of maximizing the coherence among the selected sentences, which is subject to a knapsack constraint that limits the total summary length (Keller and Wiegand, 2015). This optimization process allows us to systematically evaluate the contributions of different sentences to the coherence of the summary.

Code generation is a challenging task that has garnered significant interest from the natural language processing (NLP) and software engineering communities. With the rising tide of software applications, the importance of automated code generation is becoming increasingly evident. Traditionally, code generation is performed using general-purpose tools that aim to produce code directly from specifications or natural language descriptions. While these tools have shown impressive results in various tasks, they fall short in providing code that is tailored to the specific context of a program. In reality, source code is rarely written in isolation. It heavily depends on the programmatic context, which includes the class that the code would reside in. This context contains essential information about the expected behavior of the program, including the interfaces, data structures, and constraints that the code will interact with. Unfortunately, this context is often overlooked in code generation tasks, resulting in general-purpose code that may not align with the specific requirements of a program. To study this phenomenon, we introduce the task of generating class member functions given English documentation and the programmatic context provided by the rest of the class. This task poses several challenges. First, the desired code can vary greatly depending on the functionality the class provides. For example, a sort function may or may not be available when we are asked to "return the smallest element" in a particular member variable list. Second, the programmatic context may contain complex relationships between different classes, methods, and variables, which need to be accurately captured in the generated code. To address these challenges, we introduce CONCODE, a new large dataset with over 100,000 examples consisting of Java classes from online code repositories. Each example in the dataset contains the following: a Java class with its member variables and functions, an English documentation describing the behavior of a particular member function, and the desired code for that function. We also develop a new encoder-decoder architecture that models the interaction between the method documentation and the class environment. Our architecture is based on the transformer model (Vaswani et al., 2017), which we adapt to encode the programmatic context and the method documentation separately. The encoder part of the model takes the Java class and the method documentation as input and generates a joint representation that captures their relationship. The decoder part generates the code for the member function based on this joint representation.

Part 1: English POS Tagging Part-of-speech (POS) tagging is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP) that assigns a part-of-speech label to each word in a text. English POS tagging has been extensively studied, and several models have been proposed to tackle the problem. One of the most popular models is hidden Markov models (HMMs), which have been used to build state-of-the-art taggers. The HMM model is widely used because it can incorporate various features and is efficient to decode. However, it is well known that HMMs are based on the assumption that the world is Markovian (containing only local dependencies), but in reality, words in a sentence are highly correlated and exhibit long-range dependencies. Furthermore, many phenomena such as grammatical agreement, semantic role labeling, and verb subcategorization ignore the Markovian assumption, and will not be well captured by an HMM-based model. In this paper, we explore deterministic constraints for English POS tagging. Unlike previous approaches that only considered a few hard constraints, we formulate a constrained tagging model where we relax the constraints by assigning weights to them, giving rise to a new, more realistic, probabilistic model. By learning the weights from a training corpus, we discovered that some constraints are very informative, while others can be discarded. We utilize these constraints within the framework of structured prediction to build a constrained tagging model. By augmenting the standard Viterbi decoding algorithm, we show that this approach can be efficiently solved for large models. Moreover, we show that the constrained tagging model is more accurate than the standard model on the Penn Treebank, a widely used benchmark. Part 2: Chinese Word Segmentation Chinese word segmentation (CWS) is another fundamental NLP task in Chinese processing, and has been extensively studied over the past two decades. Unlike English, Chinese words are not separated by spaces, so word segmentation is an essential step to break the text into individual words before part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, and other NLP tasks. The task of CWS can be formulated as finding the most likely segmentation given a string of characters. Traditional approaches to CWS often rely on rule-based approaches, and machine learning methods such as conditional random fields (CRFs), and support vector machines. Although these models have achieved remarkable performance, they are still subject to errors due to the complex syntax of Chinese.

Fine-grained opinion extraction is a crucial task for sentiment analysis, allows us to better understand opinions and sentiments expressed in text and has numerous applications in customer service, marketing and natural language processing. In order to provide precise and informative opinion analysis, it is necessary to identify not only the entities that are expressing the opinions but also the specific opinions being expressed, as well as the entities that are targeted by the opinions. Opinions can be positive (e.g., "the CEO is a great leader"), or negative (e.g., "I do not like the service"). The entities expressing the opinions are called opinion holders (e.g., "I" in "I do not like the service"). Statistical machine translation (SMT) is a popular approach to natural language translation. It uses n-gram language models to predict the next word in a sentence given the context of previous words. Among various language models, continuous-space language models (CSLMs) have recently gained significant attention for their state-of-the-art performance in language modeling tasks (Mikolov et al., 2010b; Mikolov et al., 2011). CSLMs are neural network models that learn to represent the probability distribution over a vocabulary using dense vectors. The learned vectors, also known as word embeddings, have exhibited impressive capabilities in language modeling tasks, such as language modeling perplexity and automatic speech recognition. Despite their success, CSLMs are not typically used in the first pass decoding of SMT systems. The main reason for this is that the computation of the language model probabilities, which is typically performed at runtime, is slower than the computation of n-gram model probabilities, which are usually precomputed and stored in memory. One possible solution to this problem is to precompute and store the CSLM probabilities at training time, similar to what is done in the case of traditional n-gram language models. However, as pointed out in (Li et al., 2005), computing the CSLM probabilities at training time is very time-consuming. In fact, the time complexity is in the order of O(ntv), where n is the number of training examples, t is the number of tokens in the vocabulary, and v is the dimensionality of the space. This makes it impractical to store the precomputed CSLM probabilities. On the other hand, n-gram language models (NLMMs), which are commonly used in SMT, are typically trained and stored offline. Their probability computation has a linear time complexity, making it very efficient. However, n-gram language models suffer from the problem of data sparsity, where a large number of rare or unseen events are ignored. To address this problem, back-off n-gram language models (BNLMs) are trained as a hierarchical model (Jelinek et al., 1977). They are trained to predict a higher-order language model probability by backing off from a lower-order alternative when encountering an unseen sequence of words. However, the training of a BNLM from scratch is computationally expensive. In contrast, we propose a method for converting a CSLM into a BNLM, allowing the benefits of neural network based language models to be brought to the first pass decoding of SMT.

Temporal relation identification is a crucial task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), computer vision, and other areas of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Temporal relations describe the temporal relationships between events or time expressions, which can take various forms including before(B), after(A), includes(I), concurrent(C), and others. Existing work on temporal relation identification has largely focused on three types of relations: (i) the relation between an event and a time expression (absolute time), denoted as ABS; (ii) the relation between a pair of events, denoted as EVENT; (iii) the relation between an event and the document creation time, denoted as DOC. These types of relations have predominantly been identified using pairwise comparison-based approaches. The Transformer model, proposed by Vaswani et al. in 2017, has achieved state-of-the-art performance in a variety of machine translation tasks due to its ability to handle long-range dependencies and provide parallelized computation. However, the original Transformer model still has limitations when dealing with discourse phenomena, such as coherence and anaphora resolution, where document-level context is crucial. This is mainly because the Transformer model typically focuses on one sentence at a time without considering potential relationships between sentences in a document. In this work, we extend the Transformer model by incorporating a new context encoder to represent document-level context, which can improve its performance in handling discourse phenomena. Traditional machine translation models, such as phrase-based and syntax-based models, have taken advantage of the document-level context to capture more nuances of the original text, especially for languages with complex discourse structures. However, these models often ignore the subtlety of semantic relationships and the contextualization of co-references, which can significantly affect the accuracy of machine translation. The Transformer model overcomes some of these limitations by representing the input sequence as a sequence of vectors and using self-attention to compute the representation of each token by considering the entire input sequence. However, as pointed out by Tran et al. (2019), the self-attention mechanism in the original Transformer model often relies too heavily on local information, failing to capture the relationships between non-adjacent sentences in a document. In such cases, the model tends to overlook essential discourse phenomena, resulting in suboptimal translation quality. This motivated our investigation into how to provide the Transformer model with a better awareness of document-level context. To this end, we present a new context encoder that captures the essence of document-level context and incorporates it into the original Transformer encoder and decoder. The key idea is to represent the entire document as a single, flattened sequence of tokens, rather than a sequence of individual sentences, allowing the self-attention mechanism to consider the entire document when computing the representation of each token. By doing so, we enable the Transformer model to capture the relationships between non-adjacent sentences, potentially improving its performance in handling discourse phenomena. However, one significant challenge lies in training the model, since large-scale document-level parallel corpora are usually not available. In practice, abundant sentence-level parallel corpora can serve as an auxiliary training dataset, while limited document-level parallel corpora remain the primary training data.

Relation extraction is a critical task in natural language processing (NLP), with applications in information extraction, question answering, and text summarization (Mintz et al., 2009; Riedel et al., 2010). The goal of relation extraction is to identify entities and their relationships in unstructured text, such as "John Smith is the CEO of XYZ Corporation". This task is challenging due to the complexity and ambiguity of natural language, as well as the vast number of possible relations. To address these challenges, numerous approaches have been proposed, including dictionary-based methods (Ji and Grishman, 2008), kernel methods (Cao et al., 2010), distant supervision-based methods (Mintz et al., 2009) and deep learning-based methods (Zeng et al., 2014). Among these methods, distant supervision, which relies on existing knowledge graphs, has emerged as a popular approach for relation extraction (Mintz et al., 2009). The key idea of distant supervision-based methods is to leverage existing knowledge graphs, such as Freebase (Bollacker et al., 2008) and Wikidata (Vrandečić and Kraker, 2012), to automatically collect training data. With these data, the task of relation extraction becomes a classification problem: given a sentence, identify the relation between the entities mentioned in that sentence. Although distant supervision is effective in scaling relation extraction up to large-scale corpora, it inevitably suffers from the wrong labeling problem (Zeng et al., 2014). In other words, some entities in a sentence may not actually be related, but are labeled as a relation due to the noise in the knowledge graph. To address this issue, many efforts have been devoted to identifying valid instances from noisy data (Zeng et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2015; Nguyen and Nguyen, 2017). However, most existing methods handle each relation in isolation, regardless of rich semantic correlations located in relation hierarchies (Alon et al., 2019). Relation hierarchies, such as RBox (Bao et al., 2017), provide a systematic way to organize relations, with more specific relations nested under more general ones. For instance, 'type of animal' is nested under 'living thing'. Incorporating this hierarchical information of relations may help to better identify valid instances from noisy data. While existing methods can identify certain patterns within a relation, they fail to capture the nuances and permutations of relations in a hierarchy. In this paper, we aim to fill this gap by incorporating the hierarchical information of relations for distantly supervised relation extraction, and propose a novel hierarchical attention scheme.

Multi-label learning deals with a machine learning setup where each input data allows for more than one output label. Considering traditional metrics such as precision, recall, and F1-score, prior studies have demonstrated that multi-label learning can be a very challenging task due to the inherent complexities in working with many tags. In order to better understand the intricacies of group-specific learning we use the following categorisation of groups of labels that occur: (i) frequent labels occur thousands of times in the training set (frequent group); (ii) a small number of data points are available for some of these tags (few-shot group); (iii) the test set labels never occur in the training set (zero-shot group). Despite numerous studies into multi-label learning, the development of few-shot and zero-shot multi-label learning methods has primarily addressed small structured label spaces with predefined relationships between label tags by integrating the multi-label learning task with semantic relationships and dependencies in the label set. In this work, we investigate and propose few-shot and zero-shot multi-label methods to learn from large multi-label datasets with a structured label space and very few positive instances, to improve performance at the label level. We propose three few-shot methods and two zero-shot methods for learning from a large multi-label training dataset with a structured label space and incorporating certain structure in the learning process. Additionally, these can incorporate the relationships between labels in the structured label space. In particular, we make two assumptions: (i) that some labels are finer-grained than others; and (ii) that there are although unknown relationships between the labels in the structured label space, such as 'is-a', in which a finer-grained label is also a member of a coarser category. Few-shot learning has typically been examined in the multi-class and single-label scenarios, without going beyond one preceding example of a class, testing robustness to a new low-shot learning scenario where available data is limited. Social media platforms have revolutionized the way companies interact with their customers and gather insights into their opinions and behaviors. A remarkable application of social media is in understanding how users form and change their opinions about a product, and how these opinions are influenced by their friends and social networks. The field of opinion formation has received considerable attention in recent years, particularly in computer science and data analysis communities. Prior studies on opinion formation have traditionally modeled opinions as discrete or continuous sentiment values without considering the underlying semantic information (Li et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2016). However, these models ignore the intrinsic content of the posts themselves and instead focus solely on the users' sentiments or emotional reactions to certain content. In reality, opinions about a product or service are often shaped by both the content of the information and the social relationships between individuals. For instance, a user may post a positive review about a product because it is well-suited to their needs, or they may be influenced by their friends who have also expressed positive opinions about the same product. To better capture the complex factors that influence opinion formation, we propose a novel model, called the Content-based Social Influence Model, which leverages both the semantic content of social media posts and the social relationship information to model the implicit mechanism underlying the change of opinions. Machine translation (MT) has been a key area of research in natural language processing (NLP), with advances in deep learning architectures leading to significant improvements in translation quality over the past decade. However, existing MT systems often struggle to handle names, which are a crucial component of many translations. Names can be properly or improperly translated, affecting the overall quality of the translation and potentially leading to misunderstandings or misidentifications. For instance, translating the name "Liu Bei" from Chinese to English as "Liu Pie" would not only be grammatically incorrect but also change the meaning of the original sentence. Similarly, translating "Liu Bei" as "Bobby Liu" changes the emotional connotation of the sentence. In addition to name translation, the word alignment quality is another important aspect of MT that has a significant impact on downstream applications such as visualization, summarization, and question answering. Previous work on name translation and word alignment often treats names as regular words in the sentence, and ignores the unique properties of names in terms of translation and alignment. However, in Chinese-English translation, the properties such as, translation rules, translation patterns and constraints should be well respected and modeled to conduct name translation effectively, especially for proper noun translation. In this paper, we propose a Name-aware Machine Translation (MT) approach which integrates name processing into the MT model, by jointly annotating parallel corpora, extracting name-aware translation grammar and rules, adding name phrase table, and implementing name translation driven decoding. Our approach aims to enhance the quality of overall translation, name translation, and word alignment over a state-of-the-art high-quality MT baseline. Additionally, we propose a new MT metric called Informative Word-based Translation Quality (IWTQ) to effectively evaluate the translation quality of informative words in a document, by assigning appropriate weights to different words according to their importance values. This new metric will give translation quality assessors valuable insights into the translation quality of informative words, facilitating more accurate evaluation and comparison of machine translation systems. In the following, we introduce the NAMT architecture, trained with our enhanced MT baseline. Our results on Chinese-English translation demonstrate the efficacy of our name-aware approach, which shows significant improvements in translation quality, name translation, and word alignment. Specifically, our model achieves 7.4 BLEU and 4.5 ROUGE score point improvements over the baseline, showing better performance in terms of translation quality, including name translation and word alignment.

Communication plays a vital role in our daily lives. In a social setting, speakers and listeners must cooperate in order to achieve a common goal, which is to effectively convey and understand information. This cooperation is governed by the cooperative principle proposed by Grice(Grice, 1975). According to Grice, speakers are expected to make only contributions that serve the evolving conversational goals. This principle is supported by four maxims: quality (be truthful), quantity (give a little more than necessary), relevance (stay on topic) and manner (avoid ambiguity). The Gricean approach to communication provides a fundamental framework for understanding and predicting how people communicate, both in natural language and in artificial systems. However, Grice's maxims have been criticized for being too broad and vague. Furthermore, the cooperative principle has primarily been investigated using game-theoretic and linguistic accounts, but despite its central role in human communication, there is a lack of computational models that quantify and predict Gricean cooperative behavior. To address these gaps, we take a step back from the existing linguistic frameworks and draw on the theory of multi-agent decision making to model Gricean cooperative behavior. Specifically, we draw inspiration from the Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) model to demonstrate that certain Gricean principles, including the maxims of relevance, quantity and quality, can emerge as a result of individual agents' maximization of joint utility, and cooperative language use. Dec-POMDP has been used in various applications such as decision-making for multiple self-interested agents, but its application to Gricean cooperative behavior is less studied. In this paper, we investigate a multi-agent system that utilizes a belief space that models the conversational context in a way that is consistent with Grice's maxims. We propose a cognitive-inspiredgrasp of conversational reasoning-Simple- Switching(Mahmood et-al 2014 and Askarshenasa et-al2011), facilitating a sophisticateddescription of cognitiverealism for the conversational belief runs. Furthermore, we investigate how these belief models can be turned into a more formal structure that would enable us to reason about conversational utility maximization. In the following sections, we review related work, describe our model, and present experimental results showing how this formal structure emerges in the cooperative language task. As a result, we make a significant step towards modelling Gricean cooperative behavior in a formal and computationally sound way. Our findings can also have significant implications for areas such as artificial intelligence, natural language processing, and machine learning.

The task of learning to map sentences to logical form represents a fundamental challenge in natural language processing. In this problem, the goal is to develop a method that can accurately translate natural language sentences into logical representations of their meaning. Traditionally, this task has been approached through the use of hand-crafted grammars and rule-based systems. However, the complexity of natural language and the diversity of its expressions necessitate more robust and adaptive methods for learning the mappings between language and meaning. One promising approach is to leverage probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs), such as those derived from categorial grammar (CCG), to model the semantics of individual words and the compositional structure of sentences. Probabilistic CCG (CCG) grammars have the flexibility to capture a wide range of linguistic phenomena and provide a principled basis for parse tree probabilities. However, learning CCG grammars typically requires extensive manual annotation of training data or the use of domain-specific resources, which can limit their portability and applicability to other languages and meaning representations. To overcome these limitations, this paper presents a novel approach for inducing probabilistic CCG grammars from training data comprising natural language sentences paired with logical representations of their meaning. Recent advances in higher-order unification (Dowek, 1991;Rev fejasi k, 2004)open up the possibility of formulating a potentially universal framework for generating CCG parsers. Higher-order unification allows us to define the search space of grammars that are consistent with the training data and enables the construction of models that can learn to predict both the best parse for a given sentence and the probability of each possible parse. To leverage this expressive formalism, we develop an online learning algorithm that efficiently searches through the hypothesis space and simultaneously estimates the parameters of a log-linear parsing model. In contrast to previous approaches, our system is designed to be language-independent and adaptable to different meaning representations. We report high accuracy on benchmark data sets in four languages with two different meaning representations, demonstrating the potential of our method for wide-range application. The key novelties of our proposal come from: (1) the adaptation of higher-order unification to probabilistic CCG grammar learning; (2) the development of an online algorithm for efficiently searching the large hypothesis space generated by higher-order unification and (3) the implementation of a log-linear parsing model that can capture both structural relationships and the distribution of words in the input strings.

Coreference resolution is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), which identifies the mentions of the same entity or group in a text. Consider the following example, where mention A refers to the same entity as mention B:   "John mentioned that he wanted to see the John who was John the agent in the movie 'Independence Day'." In this example, the mention "John" in sentence 1 and the mention "John" in "the John who was John the agent in the movie 'Independence Day'" are coreferent. The goal of a coreference resolution system is to determine the mentions that refer to the same entity and group them together. While there are many applications of coreference resolution, such as text summarization and question answering, resolving coreference in text is often a tedious and time-consuming task. Most coreference resolution methods rely on manually annotated data for supervised learning. However, manual annotation of coreference is labor-intensive and it can take a long time to obtain a large annotated dataset. This limitation makes it challenging to apply coreference resolution to newly arising NLP problems, especially those involving limited annotations. Moreover, the current state-of-the-art models sometimes have high accuracy, especially for pronouns, though the current variants of these models find it difficult to annotate certain context-variables such as groups, different sentences as well as solved-arithmetic in numerical examples. In this context, the unsupervised setting seems appealing, and indeed some researchers have investigated unsupervised coreference resolution. However, state-of-the-art unsupervised models still lack the coreference resolution accuracy achieved by supervised methods. The goal of this paper is to present a novel, precision-oriented inference method that scores a candidate entity of a mention based on the most informative mention pair relation between the given mention entity pair in an unsupervised setting. We will introduce an informativeness score for the most precise relation of a mention entity pair regarding the coreference decisions. Our method is relatively efficient and highly accurate, especially when compared to existing state-of-the-art unsupervised coreference resolution systems. To evaluate our proposal, we implement our method within the framework of an expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm, which iteratively maximizes the likelihood function to find an optimal solution. Our unsupervised system will be put to a test on this data. Our implementation achieves significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art unsupervised methods on all benchmark data sets.

Modern automated dialog systems require a sophisticated level of semantic understanding to effectively match user input to pre-defined intents. However, the challenge of automatically identifying intent in user questions remains a significant hurdle in the development of these systems. With user questions being typically short and high-level semantic expressions, uncovering their underlying meaning can be very challenging. We propose an approach to this challenge by use of powerful semantic classifiers that are able to identify relevant features from the language input (Mitchell et al., 2003),along with incorporation of supervised clustering methods that are useful for extracting salient relationships between our classifier outputs. While there exist techniques for question retrieval (Yang et al., 2005) and question classification (Ravichandran and Hovy, 2002), little attention has been given to the task of clustering of questions into meaningful intent categories. Cluster analysis has been widely used by various researchers for the purpose of information normalization, and integration in the context of text categorization (Webber, 2001;Diao and Li, 2006;Lu et al., 2009), but the very vast space of possible question/user intent pairs poses a significant challenge for computing highly homogenous relevant subsets from the complete set of question pairs relative to the current dialog system. A major design option is to frame the problem as one of structured prediction: structured output clustering (SOC) (Chen et al., 2010a). SOC produces output that consists of a pair of cluster assignment and its internal hierarchical relations while taking account of these relationships that are although unknown at the start of the method but computed in the process of generating the cluster assignments. SOC offers several potential advantages: by describing a pair of relevant relation along with class label that distinguishes them from other pairs and by considering how these unseen relationships are computed through applying appropriate models both explicitly and in real-time. Our system leverages low-level features from the available question duplicate/matching research but discovers clusterings that reveal an underlying intent from user's highly coherent set of questions. We explore the applicability of powerful semantic classifiers from question duplicate/matching research along with a novel use of structured output within the clustering application. We perform evaluation on two labeled intent clustering datasets for two languages/domains that is to our knowledge the initial ages of their development release showing that this particular piece of our proposed model yields the best results compared with alternative question clustering approaches that remain accessible.

Aspect extraction is a critical task in sentiment analysis, aiming to identify the specific aspects of a product, service, or experience that are being discussed in customer reviews or feedback. Topic modeling has been a popular method for aspect extraction, as it can discover underlying aspects and opinions expressed in unstructured text data. However, unsupervised topic models often generate incoherent aspects due to the noisy and diverse nature of customer reviews. To address this problem, several knowledge-based models have been proposed to incorporate prior knowledge provided by the user to guide modeling, such as WordNet, domain knowledge, or hierarchical lexicons (Kim and Baldwin, 2013). The key idea is that incorporating prior knowledge can help to constrain the topic model and eliminate noisy or ambiguous topics. However, incorporating prior knowledge into a topic model requires the knowledge engineer to design and collect relevant knowledge bases, which can be time-consuming and domain-dependent. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in exploiting large amounts of Web data to learn knowledge automatically. Web data has become more abundant and diverse, providing a wide range of information, including customer reviews, product information, and social media posts. In the context of aspect extraction, learning relevant knowledge from Web data can help to identify coherent aspects and improve the overall accuracy of the topic model. This paper proposes a novel approach to learning prior knowledge automatically from a large amount of review data available on the Web. The goal is to make use of the Web as a knowledge base to improve the accuracy and coherence of aspect extraction results. However, there are two key challenges to overcome: (1) learning quality knowledge from reviews of diverse domains, and (2) making the model fault-tolerant to handle possibly wrong knowledge. The first challenge arises from the diversity of domains and the limited knowledge in specific domains. If we rely solely on the given reviews, it may not be sufficient to cover a wide range of aspects, especially for specific domains with limited knowledge. Furthermore, an inaccurate or noisy knowledge base may lead to a poor performance in aspect extraction. To address the first challenge, we will use a multi-domain approach to leverage knowledge from multiple domains. By combining knowledge from various domains, we aim to create a more comprehensive and robust knowledge base that can handle diverse domains. The second challenge of making the model fault-tolerant is essential to enable the system to handle possibly wrong knowledge.

Dependency parsing is a prominent task in natural language processing (NLP), with applications in syntax-based machine translation, information extraction, and text summarization. A common approach to dependency parsing is scoring a parse via a linear function of a set of indicator features, specifically designed to capture properties of the parse tree (Collins, 2003;McDonald et al., 2005). Designing effective features is crucial to achieve high performance on the dependency parsing task. Typically, features are manually constructed from templates applied to parts of the parse tree. The templates define which properties of a part should combine to create features, such as for instance the head of the dependency or the label of the relation. However, using only a small subset of all possible combinations is common, because manually defining all possible combinations of template functions becomes too complex and increases the number of features. Moreover, larger number of features have the potential to increase the risk of overfitting the training data. Thus it is critical to limit the number of features, which affects the dependency parsing accuracy. To overcome these issues, a novel kernel for the dependency parsing task, named Template Kernels, is presented. The Template Kernels design exploits relevant label and attribute combinations more efficiently, by including theoretically all possible feature combinations, which would be unpractical and impossible for traditional approaches. A template functions combination can be applied as a kernel over all possible set of labeled parse trees. This way, we can capture, in principle, the whole set of theoretically possible relations between the label and attribute properties that are involved in the assignment. Moreover, the kernel functions are represented by finite, closed-form expressions in terms of template functions inputs: the set of labeled parse trees is finite. In addition, integration of the kernel into a parsing reranking system is demonstrated, and its effectiveness is examined on four languages from the CoNLL-X shared task-Spanish, German, Dutch, and Czech. The results support that the proposed template kernels method is relatively efficient and highly competitive. Knowledge bases (KBs) have become increasingly abundant due to the growth of web data and crowdsourced efforts. A key challenge in maintaining and populating these KBs is the difficulty of incorporating new entities and updating existing information, a problem referred to as Knowledge Base Population (KBP). KBP involves several subtasks, including slot filling, entity group detection, relation extraction, and entity linking. Two popular KBP tasks are Cold Start Slot Filling (CSSF) and Tri-lingual Entity Discovery and Linking (TEDL). CSSF is a slot filling task in which the input is a set of entities along with data that are not sufficient to fill in their slots. Typical scenarios where this problem manifests include (1) entities that exist in the KB but are marked as "unresolved", and (2) entities that have been found recently and therefore lack sufficient information to be populated in the KB. Conversely, TEDL is a more challenging problem where the goal is to identify and link entities across multiple languages. However, more often than not, these tasks in themselves seem undoable without the collaboration of both, humans and computer algorithms. The great synergy between these two highly complimentary entities sometimes form the grounds for a heavy hearted humans though the risk of being over reliant on these machine is actually certain. Obviously, several approaches to tackle different subtasks have been proposed. However, state of the-art methods usually employ a combination of two approaches: supervised ensemble and unsupervised ensemble methods. Specifically, supervised ensemble methods utilize machine learning models that are trained on large annotated datasets and provide good performance when the amount of training data is sufficient. Examples of supervised ensemble methods include: but not limited to weighted voting, stacking, bagging and boosting (Zhang, 2009 and Breiman, 2001). However, these methods might not deliver optimal performance when there is a lack of annotated data. On the other hand, unsupervised ensemble methods utilize machine learning models that are trained only on unlabeled data, but can still provide useful predictions. Examples of unsupervised ensemble methods include: (Antczak, 2009). In this work, we propose an algorithm called CSE (Combining Supervised Ensemble) that combines both supervised and unsupervised methods to ensemble multiple systems for two KBP tasks: CSSF and TEDL. Our algorithm works as follows: Our method first trains the distribution of outputs of different machine learning models (ensemble) based on diverse sourced of high quality annotated through appropriate supervised machine learning permutations.

Distributed representations of words, alternatively known as word embeddings (Peters and Zestos, 1999;Deerwester et al., 1990), have proven to be very influential in various natural language processing (NLP) applications, demonstrating great success in improving the accuracy of many NLP models and systems. These representations assign group of features or gift to individual words, rather than encoding them with a single scalar score (Denham, 2009). One of the most significant benefits of word embeddings is their ability to alleviate data sparsity problems common in supervised learning (Manning and Schütze, 1999). The key advantage of word embeddings is that they can be induced using only unlabeled data, which is abundant for the majority of natural languages. The two most well-known algorithms for inducing these representations are word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013a, 2013b) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014). Word2vec uses a window-based technique to analyze the context in which a particular word appears, while GloVe, on the other hand, uses the distributional similarity between words to generate the word representation, as measured by various statistical methods like co-occurrence counts. In this work, we build on these representational capabilities of word embeddings to explore the idea of inducing cross-lingual representations. In other words, we aim to develop a method for creating a shared word representation space for two or more languages. This type of multilingual representation space has the potential to provide a foundation for various cross-lingual NLP applications, where a model trained on a particular language can be used for processing text from another language that is not typically seen by the model. This shared representation can simplify the cross-lingual learning problem, given that we only need to train a single set of word embeddings for all languages, rather than creating a separate set of embeddings for each language. The technical goal of our work is to treat the induction of cross-lingual word representations as a multitask learning problem (Caruana, 1997). In this problem, each task corresponds to a particular word, and task relatedness is derived from the co-occurrences of words in bilingual parallel corpora. Our view of course-lingual word representations arises from the following intuition: given that word embeddings capture linguistic regularities at the distributional level, the relationships between words across different languages should be preserved or at least consistent across the languages, which allows us to create a shared embedding space. Our choice of multitask learning as the underlying framework for our cross-lingual word embedding approach is motivated by the demand for scalable, yet interpretable learning methods in language processing (Socher et al., 2013).

Formal or informal language can have a significant impact on the meaning and interpretation of a text. Formal language is often more precise and technical, whereas informal language is usually more conversational and expressive. Consider the following text: "I thank you for the gift." "I'm totally stoked you got me the present!" The first sentence is an example of formal language, and the second sentence is an example of informal language. While both sentences convey the same meaning, they differ in their tone, vocabulary, and style. The demand for automated tools that can transform text from one style to another has been increasing over the past few decades. For instance, in many legal or business applications, transformed formal text is preferred over informally written text. On the other hand, transforming formal text into informal language can be beneficial for social media, blogs, or text messaging applications. However, meeting these needs requires the development of style transfer systems, which can transform a piece of text in one particular style into another. Despite the many benefits, significant barriers obstruct the development of such systems. One major barrier to style transfer has been the lack of proper training and evaluation datasets. The training data for style transfer consists of parallel sentences in the source and target style, meaning that each source sentence in one style has a corresponding exact translation in the target style. However, gathering parallel data is often labor-intensive, expensive, and time-consuming. Current datasets are limited to style pairs: e.g. news and informal language, news and fiction, fiction and formal business language. Moreover, most datasets although containing large collections of texts lack any indication of the style and formalities used. The goal of this paper is to present a high-quality dataset that addresses these needs by modeling the stylometric variations across a large, diverse text corpus. We present a collection of over 50,000 formal and informal language pairs drawn from Wikipedia articles. This dataset fills the gap of a wide-ranging formality stylometric training and evaluation data. We further describe and compare the performance of a range of standard models using traditional techniques from the area of translation together with convolutional and recurrent models. Our findings suggest that techniques within the community of machine translation can serve as strong baselines for this style transfer task. In evaluation, we apply standard and established metrics to the development and test splits of our datasets.

Generating high-quality paraphrases is a crucial task for various NLP applications, including text summarization, question answering, and machine translation (Rush et al., 2015;Wang et al., 2017;Gan et al., 2019). Recent advances in paraphrase generation have mainly relied on the encoder-decoder framework, with the exception of some work on multi- task learning (Zhou et al., 2018) and post-processing techniques (Budzianowski et al., 2019). However, these models suffer from a major limitation: they tend to memorize the words and patterns in the training dataset instead of learning the meaning of the words. As a result, the generated sentences often lack semantic correctness and coherence, even if they are syntactically correct. In an attempt to address this issue, this paper proposes a novel approach to paraphrase generation, using a Word Embedding Attention Network (WEAN) that combines the strengths of encoder-decoders and neural word embeddings. Unlike traditional models that rely solely on pre-trained word embeddings, our proposed approach treats word embeddings as a query space and perform a sorting process that samples highly-ranked word relevant to the given source text upon each decoding step. In doing so, our model avoids overreliance on the training data and improves the semantic quality of generated paraphrases. Specifically, we designed the WEAN model to incorporate the following refinements to the basic encoder-decoder framework: Firstly, the encoder first generates a fixed-length vector to characterize the source text. This is done by taking the maximum or average over the output of a feed-forward network with shared weights. Secondly, the decoder is modified to generate the next word by querying the word embeddings and sampling from the output of a softmax layer with temperature control. We hope that this query-and-output process can learn the meaning of the words more effectively, and the paraphrases generated can exhibit higher semantic coherence. Thirdly, an additional neural module is added to model the semantic coherence of the generated paraphrases, thereby guiding the generation process more effectively. Furthermore, we extend our proposed WEAN model to the two different paraphrase-oriented tasks, namely text simplification and short text abstractive summarization. By leveraging these two tasks, our model outperforms state-of-the-art models on this wide range of paraphraseoriented NLP tasks by a significant margin. Sentiment analysis deals with the prediction of sentiment polarity (positive, negative, or neutral) from text, with applications in various domains (Davidson et al., 2010;Kiritchenko et al., 2014). Traditional sentiment analysis approaches typically view sentiment as a single entity to be classified (Kim and Hovy, 2004), with tasks often being confined to a single domain or genre (Brants andNazarian, 2001;Wilson et al., 2005). However, sentiment analysis can be more accurately modelled by taking into account underlying topics related to the expressed sentiment (Zhuang et al., 2006). Joint sentiment-topic (JST) models were recently proposed to model this relationship between sentiment and topics (Deng et al., 2018), allowing for a more sophisticated understanding of text with both sentiment and topic information. The JST model learns latent topics and corresponding sentiment labels in an unsupervised manner, using domain-independent polarity word priors for weekly supervised signals. JST model learns from large-scale unlabeled text and automatically identifies sentiment-bearing topics from text, thereby reveals the underlying topic-wise sentiment semantics. Nevertheless, training the JST model remains challenging, especially for cross-domain sentiment classification tasks, requiring multiple domain datasets. Furthermore, another key challenge of the cross-domain task is the different distribution of topics between domains. Since topics can potentially change from domain to domain, employing topic features from learned topic-word distribution, even with the high dimensionality of features, may lead to low transfer ability and although successful adaptation models can address this limitation but often require difficult parameter tuning. Moreover, without using sufficient training data from each single domain, a separate model trained for individual supervised domain tasks can also not capture common underlying semantics and shared targets between multiple unseen domains. To address these limitations, in this work, we extend the JST model by augmenting the topic distributions using word polarity priors. We found that this modification helps to more proficiently capture the highly correlated sentiment meanings behind the topics to the seen, thereby enhances the generalizability of learned polarity-bearing topics to new domains and makes full use of the unique aspects of each domain to enrich its learned topic representations. Based on this observation, our primary contributions in this paper can be listed below: 1. We proposed a more informative and extendable topic representations obtained by incorporating word polarity priors into word-topic Dirichlet priors, which allows the latent topics of the input text to capture high-level abstract concepts of sentiment.

Language models are a critical component of many natural language processing (NLP) applications, such as speech recognition, machine translation, and text summarization. They are typically implemented as n-gram models, where the probability of a word being emitted given its n-1 preceding words is estimated based on a large corpus of text. N-gram language models have several advantages over other models, including simplicity, effectiveness, and ease of implementation. However, as the size of the corpus increases, the size of the n-gram model also grows, leading to increased memory requirements and slower query times. This is because the model needs to store data for every possible n-gram in the corpus, which can result in a large number of entries. One way to mitigate this problem is to use more efficient data structures to represent the n-gram model. In general, a language model comprises three main components: the vocabulary, the n-gram table, and the arithmetic coder. The vocabulary is a set of unique words in the language, and the n-gram table stores the count of each n-gram in the corpus. The arithmetic coder is used to perform arithmetic coding and decoding of the linguistic entropy of the input data, and is driven by the n-gram table and the probability distributions it contains. Hash tables have been traditionally used to represent the n-gram table, as they allow for fast lookup and insertion operations. However, they can still consume a lot of memory, especially for large corpora. In this work, we explore an alternative data structure, the double-array, which has shown promising results in representing large-scale n-gram language models. The double-array is a sparse array data structure that uses two arrays, one for words and the other for word counts, to represent a dictionary. This data structure has been shown to be highly efficient in terms of memory usage and query speed. Moreover, it can handle large-scale dictionaries with tens of millions of entries. In this paper, we describe a highly efficient method for implementing n-gram language models using double-array structures. We first address the problem of representing backwards suffix trees using double-array structures. Backwards suffix trees are used to store the n-gram counts for each word in the vocabulary. By using double-array structures to represent the backwards suffix trees, we can achieve a significant reduction in memory usage compared to the traditional hash table approach.
