Sentiment analysis, a crucial task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), has been extensively applied in various domains such as product review, tweets, and social media platforms to predict the user's perception or attitude towards a product, service, or idea. With the ever-growing amount of user-generated content, the quality and reliability of sentiment analysis systems have become increasingly important. However, classic sentiment analysis techniques are limited by the ignoring of user and product contexts that significantly influence the meaning and intensity of text (Li et al., 2010;Hu et al., 2013). To address these issues, incorporating user and product information into traditional sentiment analysis models has been shown to be beneficial (Keshtkar et al., 2017;Liu et al., 2017), especially in cases where the number of reviews for users or products with limited reviews is not sufficient to train robust models, i.e. the cold-start problem in recommendation systems (Berkovsky et al., 2010). The difficulty of handling the cold-start problem mainly stems from the limited availability of user and product information which is pivotal to traditional collaborative filtering methods (Resnick et al., 1994). As relevant user and product embeddings are essential for various NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, previous research has focused on incorporating certain context-agnostic representations, such as word embeddings (W3R14) and bag of words (W3O14). However, such simple methods, although efficient, fail to capture the subtle semantic relations between users and products and are prone to over-smoothing due to the dimension reduction process (Li et al., 2016). Recently, more progressed approaches like graph-based methods (Gao et al., 2017) and multi-task learning (Zhang et al., 2020) have been proposed to represent both users and products, nevertheless, they often rely on complex compositional frameworks and numerous hyperparameters to be fine-tuned, and thus lack an intuitive understanding of latent relations and suffer from a slow training process to accommodate large-scale datasets. Moreover, most of these sophisticated approaches ignore the distributional disparities across cold-start and well-start user/product documents, causing poor performance in cold-start scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose Hybrid Contextualized Sentiment Classifier (HCSC), consisting of a fast word encoder and Cold-Start Aware Attention (CSAA) for efficient and accurate sentiment classification with a focus on handling the cold-start problem effectively. The next section describes the proposed architecture and model details in-depth through discussing the fastword encoder and the mechanism of CSAA.

Automatic keyphrase extraction is a crucial task in content analysis and summarization, which identifies the most relevant phrases from a given text that summarize its main ideas. Recently, n-gram-based evaluation metrics have emerged as promising alternatives to traditional metrics such as precision, recall, and F-score. These metrics evaluate the quality of extracted keyphrases by calculating the n-gram similarity between the extracted keyphrases and the gold standard keyphrases. However, most existing studies on n-gram-based evaluation metrics have been conducted in the context of machine translation and summarization, and little is known about their effectiveness in automatic keyphrase extraction. To bridge this gap, this study investigates the feasibility of adapting various n-gram-based evaluation metrics to automatic keyphrase extraction. The adapted metrics are based on language modeling and n-gram similarity, including BLEU, Meteor, and R-precision. The performance of the adapted metrics is evaluated on a gold standard keyphrase extraction dataset. We also compare the performance of the adapted metrics with that of traditional metrics such as precision, recall, and F-score. Our results show that R-precision, which measures the proportion of the extracted keyphrases that contain at least one word from the gold standard keyphrases, achieves the highest correlation with human annotations. Furthermore, we analyze the degree of semantic similarity between the extracted keyphrases and the gold standard keyphrases. We propose a novel framework for evaluating the semantic similarity between keyphrases, which takes into account the location of partially-matching component words. Our results show that the degree of semantic similarity varies with the location of the partially-matching component words, suggesting that more flexible n-gram matching strategies may be required to achieve high-quality keyphrase extraction results. To better understand the relationship between the adapted metrics and keyphrase extraction quality, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the correlation between the adapted metrics and human annotations. Our results indicate that the adapted metrics are highly correlated with human annotations, but the correlation is not always monotonic. This suggests that the adapted metrics may capture some aspects of keyphrase extraction quality that are not captured by traditional metrics such as precision, recall, and F-score. In conclusion, our study shows that adapted n-gram-based evaluation metrics can be effective in automatic keyphrase extraction, and highlights the importance of accounting for near-misses currently ignored by standard evaluation metrics. Our results also demonstrate the potential of R-precision as a highly effective evaluation metric for automatic keyphrase extraction.

The domain of natural language processing (NLP) has witnessed a tremendous rise in the application of ontologies for knowledge representation and inference (Hoffman and Hunt, 2007). Ontologies, which provide structured knowledge about concepts, relationships, and instances, have been used extensively in NLP tasks, such as information extraction (Pustejovsky et al., 2006), sentiment analysis (Brody et al., 2009), and semantic role labeling (Gildea and Jurafsky, 2002). However, evaluating and improving ontologies to support NLP tasks remains a challenging and open problem. Current methods for evaluating the quality of an ontology focus on calculating metrics, such as the number of instances, coverage, and consistency (Gangemi et al., 2002), that provide insights into the ontology's structural properties. These metrics are useful but lack the ability to assess the ontology's content and relevance in a particular domain. In this paper, we present a novel methodology for evaluating and improving ontologies using spreading activation over a graph that represents instances of ontology concepts and relationships in a target domain, to support NLP tasks, such as word-sense disambiguation (WSD). Recent advances in NLP have exhibited the immense potential of word-sense disambiguation for capturing the nuances of human language and facilitating various applications, including question answering, text classification, and language modeling (Agirre et al., 2009). The representation of word meaning has been a long-standing problem in the field of linguistics and artificial intelligence. Traditional approaches to studying semantic representation rely heavily on linguistic information, such as co-occurrence patterns and lexical definitions, assuming that word meaning can be learned solely from the linguistic environment. However, a growing body of evidence from various disciplines, including psychology, neuroscience, and philosophy, suggests that language is grounded in perception and action (Barsalou, 2008;Gentner, 1982). This idea has led to a reconceptualization of semantic representation, emphasizing the role of sensorimotor experience in shaping word meaning. The notion of grounded cognition posits that abstract concepts, including those represented by words, are derived from concrete perceptions and bodily experiences (Wilson, 2002). In this context, researchers have started to explore the integration of linguistic and perceptual data to create more comprehensive models of semantic representation. One promising approach is to use naturally occurring corpora to approximate linguistic information, such as co-occurrence patterns and lexical definitions (Turian et al., 2010). Perceptual data can be approximated using feature norms, which capture the attributes native speakers consider important in describing the meaning of a word (Kilner et al., 2012). For example, the concept of "dog" can be associated with attributes such as "furry," "four-legged," and "friendly." By leveraging both linguistic and perceptual data, researchers can create more nuanced and sophisticated models of word meaning. However, the integration of linguistic and perceptual data poses significant challenges, such as mitigating noise and idiosyncrasies in the data, and determining how to combine the two modalities in a principled manner. In this paper, we present a comparative study of several models that represent word meaning based on linguistic and perceptual data. The models differ in terms of the mechanisms by which they integrate the two modalities, ranging from simple concatenation to more complex hierarchical combinations. We evaluate the models using human data, including similarity judgments and classification tasks, to assess their ability to capture the nuances of word meaning. Our results suggest that a closer correspondence to human data can be obtained by uncovering latent information shared among the textual and perceptual modalities, rather than arriving at semantic knowledge by concatenating the two. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of semantic representation and highlight the importance of considering the interplay between linguistic and perceptual data in modeling word meaning. Machine translation (MT) parameter tuning is a well-established task in natural language processing. The goal of this task is to optimize the model parameters of a statistical machine translation system given a set of acquisition functions (Chiang et al., 2007) that measure the quality of the translations. Some popular optimization methods for this task are Hill Climbing (Weston et al., 2003), MERT (Och, 2003) and Bayesian optimization (Wang et al., 2015). Despite their widespread usage, however, these approaches have some drawbacks. Hill Climbing processes acquisition functions sequentially and can therefore be slow for optimization of many parameters. MERT is limited to optimizing a small subset of parameters (typically 20) (Casacuberta and Marino, 2011) and finds a good approximation of the optimal with predefined hyperparameters. Bayesian optimization, on the other hand, explores the parameter space by acquiring a fixed set of acquisition points in each iteration, and is known for its inefficiency in high-dimensional parameter spaces. To overcome these issues, a few approaches based on the MIRA algorithm of Crammer and Singer (Crammer and Singer, 2003) have lately been proposed (Watanabe et al., 2007;Chiang et al., 2008b). These methods, although promising, may still not be as efficient as we would desire. In practice they may still use a predefined, and sometimes fixed, number of iterations. This number is often chosen according to experiments that end although there are no solid reasons why they end when they do and this is also another point in favor of our proposition. We propose to steer around these issues by implementing a novel method that exploits the pairwise approach to ranking (Herbrich et al., 1999). Specifically, our pairwise ranking optimization (PRO) method formulates the parameter tuning problem as the ranking of system configurations with respect to their quality scores. This is achieved through the histogram cost function (HHF), a convex upper bound on the best rank (Alon et al., 2005). A critical advantage of PRO is the ability to leverage off-the-shelf software for solving the ranking problem, making it very easy to implement and apply to any machine translation system. Another key benefit of this approach is scalability and this is where the pairwise nature of the ranking algorithm plus the implementation of a small subset of viel the distribution of pairwise comparasons of the evaluations (often zero based evaluations) come in handy. We establish PRO's effectiveness and desirability in practice by comparing it to state-of-the-art optimization methods including MERT (Och, 2003) and MIRA (Watanabe et al., 2007) in a number of language pairs.

Neural machine translation (NMT) models have emerged as a state-of-the-art approach to machine translation. They achieve this by automatically learning the relationship between input and output languages, without explicit acquisition of linguistic rules and patterns, unlike rule-based machine translation models and statistical machine translation models. Recently, sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models with attention mechanism incorporated have achieved promising results, making NMT more attractive and popular compared to traditional statistical machine translation models like phrase-based statistical machine translation (PBSMT) models. Meanwhile, numerous modifications have been proposed to improve the performance of NMT models. However, the most widely adopted data-driven optimization approach, the teacher forcing method (Williams and Zipser, 1989), still suffers from exposure bias (Ranzato et al., 2016), the main cause of which is that this standard word-level training method cannot enable the model to predict the correct target word when conditioned on the correct previously predicted target words. The teacher forcing algorithm predicts the next word directly based on the current input sentence and hypothetical previous predicted target words, rather than the correct previously predicted target words, thereby introducing the exposure bias that can severely limit the sequence-level understanding of NMT models. In other words, when a word is generated based on the previous word, the ability to generate the subsequent word will become imperfect due to the flaws in the previously generated word. Concretely, suppose the goal is to translate: (premise,Asian civilization): Here originated many philosophers. (hypothesis,in XX century): Ishibumi did extremely talent. If the model incorrectly generates the first word: in, although it matches with the template i(the: but ) a clan of sensational thinker., the hypothesis will undoubtedly go off track with a wrong beginning i(in XX ). Therefore, the reinforcement framework proposed in (Ranzato et al., 2016) demonstrates that sequence-level training can alleviate the exposure bias issue. However, due to the high variance of the gradient histogram estimation and poor interpretability, sequence-level training using the reinforcement framework for NMT has given up. Furthermore, (Li et al., 2016) tryed to overcome the exposure bias through incorporating softmax selection policy for training NMTs but the computational complexity raises significantly. Inspired by (Peters et al., 2017), this work attempts to improve the NMT performance by reformulating the optimization objectives with a differentiable distribution-based sequence-level training objective on probabilistic n-gram matching. This model inherently avoids the issues in the existing approaches to sequence-level training, yet efficiently enables the gradient back propagation through both the sequence distributions and word-based conditional distributions, solving the limitation of prior works following the reinforcement framework)}}.

In recent years, natural language processing (NLP) has witnessed tremendous progress in various tasks such as language understanding, machine translation, and text summarization. A crucial challenge in advancing NLP is the efficient acquisition and application of knowledge from different sources. One approach to bridging this gap is by leveraging the human-curated knowledge encoded in linguistic rules, primarily in the form of entailment and paraphrase rules. Entailment rules capture semantic relationships between words or phrases, thereby providing a precursor to deeper understanding of their meaning. On the other hand, paraphrase rules associate semantically related expressions. By combining these rules, we can advance the foundations of many NLP tasks. However, as the number of rules increases, so does the computational complexity of their combined application, which often results in slow and memory-intensive inference processes. For instance, given a word " small",ruler"live_in small house if you are poor and rule p"I live in a small house" can give out p"I am poor". In other words, more efficiency in this application is needed in order to perform various NLP tasks more accurately, such as question answering and text classification. Efficient inference is highly desirable as it directly impacts the scalability and effectiveness of various NLP applications. Unfortunately, the existing approach does not provideefficacies for inference with large-scale knowledge. In fact, the efficiency issue is a long-standing challenge in this field. In light of this, developing a scalable and efficient method for applying entailment and paraphrase rules is of paramount importance. To address this challenge, we propose a data structure called the Compact Forest and a corresponding algorithm. The goal of this data structure is to efficiently capture the relationships between words or phrases by modeling them as a tree-like structure. Our algorithm combines and prunes the trees in such a way that the statements of given inference rules are efficiently retrieved. This new data-structure consists of two binary trees:The Restrictive Forest that keeps track of primitive properties of words and the redundant forest facilitating the rule application process to the words, thereby forming the tolerant factor together. The reason why we want to come out with this data-structure is that many inference rules rely on word sense information, which is becoming increasingly valuable. Moreover, trees as a data structure ages to offer a drastic improvement in the view of both the quantity of data and the efficiency compared with maintaining several tables as that of traditional databases.

Tokenization is a critical preprocessing step for many NLP tasks, including machine translation. However, tokenization can be more challenging for certain languages such as Chinese and Korean due to their complex writing systems and syntactic structures. As a result, tokenization errors can potentially introduce translation mistakes for translation systems relying on 1-best tokenizations. Traditionally, tokenization is done as a preprocessing step, followed by translation. However, this sequential approach poses a problem since translation mistakes can then be carried over to the tokenization step. While lattices (Och, 1999;Och and Ney, 2002) have been used in many machine translation (MT) systems as an alternative to 1-best translations, they have limitations when it comes to depth and width. Furthermore, not all components of a translation system (e.g., word alignment, language modeling) can be modified to utilize lattice information, and handling lattices can be resource-intensive. Our proposal is a variant of the sequence-to-sequence models commonly used in deep learning based MT (Bengio et al., 2015;Vinyals et al., 2015). Moses, Koehn et al. (2007), is a state-of-the-art open-source toolkit for statistical machine translation and consists of a transfer, reordering, lexicalized syntax-based sentence model, and features a backend integration with decoder. However, Moses recipients of two input expressions only, and as such, fails to leverage both the source and target expressions for solutions to deeply challenging although straightforward problems found in some MT systems. So, we take the even more radical approach of doing tokenization and translation jointly. We introduce a sequence-to-sequence model that learns to produce not only a translation, but also a tokenization simultaneously. This approach handles imperfect tokenization in source text in a principled way. This architecture forms a single network, with an encoder that reads the input sequence, and a decoder that produces the aligned and tokenized translation. The encoder encodes the input sequence, and for each position in the queue, our joint decoder predicts the token and translation for that position. This dual prediction structure has two outputs: a softmax output for predicting the translation probabilities, and a discrete output for token prediction. Our model is trained by minimizing a sequence of two sequence problems where the decoder tries to jointly produce several tokens and a translation for the source input at the same time. Our experiments on the Chinese-English and Korean-Chinese datasets show that this can be done efficiently, achieving top performance.

Semantic role labeling (SRL) is a crucial task in natural language processing (NLP), which aims to identify the roles that entities play in a sentence and describe the meaning of that sentence. Among existing lexical resources that provide SRL annotations, PropBank and NomBank are two well-known ones. PropBank (Palmer et al., 2005) is a large-scale lexicon that annotates predicates with their semantic roles and arguments. NomBank (Grishman and Sterling, 2006) provides SRL annotations for nominal predicates, which accounts for a significant portion of predicates in language. However, both PropBank and NomBank have their own limitations. PropBank focuses primarily on verb-based annotations, while NomBank covers predicate nominal (PN) and action nominal (AN) predicates. Therefore, recognizing both resources can significantly enhance the performance of SRL systems. Furthermore, the advent of deep learning has seen a boost in the performance of various NLP tasks, including SRL. Contemporary SRL systems have typically been based on traditional machine learning methods or deep learning methods such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks. These models sometimes have high accuracy, especially for specific cases, though the risk of overfitting is high. Traditional SRL pipelines have cascaded off-the-shelf parts-of-speech taggers, parsers, and SRL models. Such a pipeline structure is simple but only allows standalone, single-task processes to be composed. In some cases, this type of system does not work extremely well. There are several recent studies aiming to integrate the information from both PropBank and NomBank. Some of these works introduce new argument labels to annotate frames from both PropBank and NomBank. 1 Feature selection is one of the most crucial tasks for building a high-performance machine learning model. Many random feature selection methods are used to choose the optimal set of features. 2 In recent years, large-scale feature selection has gained significant attention. Deep learning models have engendered substantial performance gains for numerous tasks. Some research focuses on efficient integration of PropBank and NomBank through a shallow or a deep structure. 3 These research studies can provide a good starting point for our work to integrate PropBank and NomBank. In this paper, we put forward a new approach to enhance the performance of the SRL system by integrating information from both PropBank and NomBank. We achieve this by utilizing a combination of pre-trained based partparsers and two high-performance SRL systems, which can complete a robust integrated SRL system with competitive performance.

The online news landscape is a vast and diverse content sector with a huge number of news articles being published every day. Under this circumstance, it is nowadays more and more difficult for individuals to keep up with the latest news and gain a comprehensive understanding of current events. As an assistance tool, the news overview article is useful for people to quickly get the gist of major news and events and to understand the related context. However, writing a good news overview article typically requires human editors' professional knowledge, manual content selection and composition skills, and a lot of time spent on curating news content. This processes make news overview articles manually generated and manually summarized available in many well-known news websites less frequently as the number of new article grows. In addition, generating news overview articles is time-consuming, labor-intensive and extremely expensive. Therefore, an automated method for generating news overview articles is essential to enable people to have quicker and more accessible ways of getting the latest news and trends. In this paper, we investigate a new task of automatically constructing an overview article from a given set of news articles about a news event, focusing on passage ranking, passage selection and passage fusion. The objective of automatic construction of news overview articles is to create a complete and concise overview of a given news event based on multiple original news articles to help readers quickly understand the event. The core steps in this task are preprocessing, passage extraction, passage ranking, passage composition, and final summarization of the overall article, and as our primary contribution, we introduce the news synthesis approach as outlined above by adding the although straightforward extremely important passage fusion technique which essentially belongs to the topic selection in terms of news viewponts. Our proposed news synthesis approach is compared with several popular multi-document summarization methods, including Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA), Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), and LexRank on the Wikinews-SUM-CONTACT dataset 2, and achieves the best performance on both automatic evaluation and manual evaluation. The remaining part of this paper is organized as follows: we first introduce the related work and background knowledge about multi-document summarization, passage fusion and news view point. Then, we specify our proposed news synthesis approach, which consists of four sub-modules: passage extraction, passage ranking, passage selection and passage fusion. Next, we describe the experiment settings and evaluation metrics used in this paper.

Unsupervised learning of relations and patterns is a central task in natural language processing, particularly in relation extraction. Relation Extraction (RE) is a nowadays well-studied task that refers to the process where a text-span, typically a sentence or phrase, is identified as a relation instance of a certain type, like "was-born" or "treats-illness." Most existing approaches to RE require large amounts of manually annotated training data for each desired relation type. However, getting this type of gold-standard data can be a time-consuming and expensive process. The demand for more automatic processes and scalable systems that can discover and extract multiple relation types, even the ones that have not been observed before, has grown in recent times. Unsupervised Relation Extraction (URE) is a branch of RE that tries to handle these issues by using clustering methods to discover a priori unknown relations on the top of patterns that are learned from unlabeled data. This learning setting is in-line with the general unsupervised weekly, which means that more efficiency in this direction could shift in short run the existing manually annotation packages more towards automated, mainstream approach for identified entities in text. A well-known technique to discover binary relations among entities in text involves the clustering of pairs of entities based on their semantic similarity, which in turn is often captured using word embeddings. For instance, we could cluster entity pairs based on their similarity by taking the dot product of their respective vector representations. More generally, URE methods can be categorized along a dimension describing the kind of information used to capture the similarity between entity pairs, with word embeddings and distributed word representations forming one end of this spectrum. They represent words and entities in a dense vector space where semantically similar entities are located close to one another. At the other end of this spectrum we find more structural representations that often do not make use of word representations to model the semantic similarity between entity pairs. An example for this category are certain subtypes of dependency-based representations. In these representations, the similarity between entities is captured based on the way they are connected through a parse tree. For instance, two entity pairs are often closer in the vector representation of the dependency relations where the predicate argument chain is similar.

Comparison of sentences is a fundamental operation in Natural Language Processing (NLP). It is essential to various NLP tasks such as paraphrase identification, question answering, retrieval and classification, etc. Throughout the years, several methods have been proposed for sentence comparison, with varying success in terms of accuracy and efficiency (Socher et al., 2013;Vendrov et al., 2015;Severyn and Moschitti, 2015;Logeswaran and Srivastava, 2018). However, most of these methods focus solely on word-level comparison. While word-level features can capture some surface-level coherency between the two input sentences, they fail to capture deeper semantic relationships (Kordjamshidi et al., 2014), therefore limiting their generalizability and performance. On the other hand, modeling at the sentence-level, through the use of entire sentence embeddings, can capture more abstract semantic coherency between sentences, but does not provide any insight into the compositional structure of the sentences. For example, in cases where the sentences are semantically similar, but structured in a different way, a sentence-level model may generalize well, but would fail to capture the underlying differences in structure. In order to capture these structural relationships, researchers have proposed certain methodologies for incorporating sentence structure into the comparison task (Titov and McDonald, 2008;Mettler and Strube, 2010;Asghar et al., 2015;Wang et al., 2018;Yu et al., 2018). These methodologies typically involve either: (i) applying a tree-bank parser to obtain a parse tree for each sentence, which is then used in conjunction with the similarity measure, (ii) using pre-trained models such as dependency tree representations, or (iii) generating synthetic trees using recursive neural networks (RNNs). However, learning sentence structure through a pre-processing step increases the risk of errors being propagated into the model. Moreover, the incorporation of the tree structures in the similarity measures can significantly increase the computational cost of these methods. This makes them impractical for large-scale applications where the need for scalability is paramount. In this work, we propose a different approach that directly aligns two sentences by discovering their latent tree structures. We leverage the power of structured attention mechanisms, which have previously been used in a variety of applications, such as machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2015) and text summarization (Rush et al., 2015), to match candidate spans in the first sentence to candidate spans in the second sentence, while simultaneously discovering the tree structure of each sentence. Our model, which we refer to as a structured alignment network (SAN), directly matches the tree structures and thus achieves the comparison of sentences without pre-processing the sentence structures.

Terminology acquisition from comparable corpora has become a central task in natural language processing (NLP), notably for knowledge-based and multilingual applications. Considerable attention has been given to identifying equivalent terms in monolingual corpora, including impact assessments, dictionary updates and cross-lingual knowledge sharing. The importance of punctuation in natural language processing is well established [Jurafsky and Martin, 2000]. Even the most basic text processing tasks, such as part-of-speech tagging and parsing, require accurate punctuation information as a basic preprocessing step. To address this problem, a range of methods have been proposed for predicting punctuation marks from either raw or perplexity scores of automatic speech recognition (ASR) outputs [Zhu et al., 2013, Qin and Meng, 2017, Shen et al., 2018]. However, the existing methods are plagued by several limitations. Firstly, the most popular approaches exploit limited contextual information with predefined fixed length context windows [Zhu et al., 2013, Qin and Meng, 2017], which cannot always capture the long-range dependencies for punctuation prediction. However, more complex models that can fully exploit global context and perform accurate punctuation prediction is more challenging, since mainstream methods for punctuation prediction [Zhu et al., 2013, Qin and Meng, 2017, Shen et al., 2018] either need to chunk certain context for post-processing, or have different sentences as input preprocessing, resulting high complexity, potentially resulting in time-consuming prediction processes. Event extraction is a critical task in natural language processing (NLP), with applications in information extraction, question answering, and text summarization. The task involves identifying specific events or actions described in text, where an event is defined as a happening or action that has some effect on entities. For Chinese event extraction, the process of event extraction is particularly challenging due to the use of complex linguistic structures, polysemous words, and lack of annotated resources (Xu et al., 2003). Chinese event extraction systems generally involve two key sub-tasks: trigger identification and event type determination (Sundheim, 2000). Trigger identification involves identifying the verb or action that describes the event, whereas event type determination requires identifying the type or category of the event, which can be social, political, governmental, etc. In reality, these two sub-tasks are closely interrrelated, and the quality of one sub-task will impact the results of the other. However, most previous studies tend to treat these sub-tasks separately, using independent models for each task (Wang and Fan, 2006;Fan, 2011). Nevertheless, a key characteristic that is highly underestimated is relevant for high accuracy, especially for languages such as Chinese: event type and trigger interaction. Furthermore, another key challenge of Chinese event extraction is the low quality of annotated event corpora. Since annotated event data has limited availability, we rely on weakly annotated data with lower precision, with the prerequisite that the task completion requires noise-tolerant solutions (Pradhan et al., 2005). In addition, the high ratio of pseudo trigger mentions to true ones in the event corpora also poses a challenge for event extraction systems (Chiticariu et al., 2009). To address these issues, this paper proposed a novel approach, called Joint Modeling of Trigger Identification and Event Type Determination, consists of two main components. First, a joint model of trigger identification and event type determination is designed to model the interaction between triggers and event types. By jointly modeling the two sub-tasks, our model can capture the complex patterns between triggers and events. This will reduce errors that would have been produced by dealing with triggers and events separately. Moreover, to filter out as many pseudo trigger mentions as possible, several trigger filtering schemas are introduced to this joint model. The evaluations on the ACE 2005 Chinese corpus show that our proposed approach significantly outperftoms a strong baseline, demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed model in refining event extraction systems, which can desirably decrease the pseudo trigger ratio.

Machine translation (MT) system combination has been widely used to improve translation performance by leveraging the strengths of multiple MT systems (Koehn et al., 2007). Among various approaches to MT system combination, confusion network (CN) decoding has shown the best performance in recent years (Chao and/player). CN decoding represents each MT system group with a confusion network, which can seamlessly combine the output hypotheses from multiple MT systems and discard the divergence in translations. However, one of the most significant challenges in CN decoding remains the hypothesis alignment between different MT systems. The difficulty lies in that multiple MT systems may order the identical words differently, resulting in many-to-many alignments. Consequently, there is an overwhelming number of possible word alignments, which makes it challenging to determine the correct hypothesis-word alignment and extremely difficult to find a reliable hypothesis alignment (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005). In the past, several word alignment methods have been proposed to handle the above problem, but the performance is inconsistent and highly dependent on the quality of the word alignment model (Koehn et al., 2007). In this paper, we compare the hypothesis alignment results using four widely used word alignment methods, namely, GIZA++ (Och and Ney, 2003), TER (Snover et al., 2004), CLA (Li et al., 2011) and IHMM (Och and Ney, 2002). Our results show that different word alignment methods yield significantly different performances in hypothesis alignment, and the quality of the alignment has a direct impact on the overall performance of CN decoding. To address the challenge of improving the reliability of hypothesis alignment, we propose a novel method, which utilizes the intersection of direct and inverse alignments between the backbone and hypothesis. This intersection word alignment (IWA) is motivated by the fact that direct and inverse alignments between two sentences are paired words, meaning that if a word in the direct alignment has an alignment to another word in the inverse alignment, it indicates that these two words are likely to be the same given their sentence contexts. The idea of combining direct and inverse alignments has contributed to a significant reduction in word alignment errors, which can provide a more reliable hypothesis alignment for CN decoding. We evaluate the proposed IWA method using two benchmarks: Chinese-to-English spoken and written language translation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that IWA yields consistent performance improvements for all the four word alignment methods used in hypothesis alignment, which indicates that IWA can be a robust and reliable method for hypothesis alignment in MT system combination.

In recent years, natural language processing (NLP) has witnessed tremendous progress with the advent of deep learning techniques. These techniques have led to the development of various NLP architectures that are highly effective in performing various tasks, such as parsing, semantic role labeling, and machine translation. Despite the significant advances, most NLP systems are designed with a fixed directionality of information flow. For instance, in a typical NLP pipeline, the parser is followed by the semantic role labeler (SRL). The parser provides the SRL with a parse tree, and the SRL identifies the semantic roles of the verbs in the sentence. While this unidirectional flow of information is often sufficient, it is not the only way to interconnect NLP components. The possibility of bidirectional information flow between NLP components has not been fully explored, and with the current trend towards multi-task learning and deep neural networks, it is an area that warrants investigation. This paper attempts to fill this gap by investigating how a parser can benefit from a semantic role labeler and vice versa. The main contribution of this work is to propose a novel approach to utilizing semantic role predictions in parsing. Specifically, we design a system that reranks the parse trees generated by a parser based on their predicted semantic roles. In this system, we utilize an averaged perceptron model to distinguish likely semantic roles from erroneous ones. We then use this model to penalize parses that give rise to low-scoring semantic roles. This reranking process is the key innovation of our approach and allows us to leverage the strengths of the parser and the SRL in a more collaborative manner. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. In particular, we report two sets of experiments. The first set involves reranking n-best parses generated by a baseline generative model using our proposed model. We find that this reranking process significantly improves the accuracy of the predicted semantic roles. The second set involves predicting semantic roles at parse time using an augmented version of our SRL model. By forcing the parser to produce parses that are likely to give rise to high-scoring semantic roles, we are able to further improve the accuracy of our SRL model. The key finding of this paper is that the joint consideration of parsing and semantic role labeling can lead to improvements in both components. Our results show that the proposed approach yields better performance than the SRL model that is trained on the parses generated by the baseline parser.

Information retrieval is a challenging task that involves searching for relevant documents in a large corpus based on a user's query. Traditional information retrieval models rely on terms and their frequencies to match the user's query with documents in the corpus. However, these models often fail to capture the nuanced relationships between terms and their subtleties, resulting in incomplete or irrelevant retrieval results. In an effort to address these limitations, researchers have proposed various techniques that incorporate semantic relationships between terms into the information retrieval process. A key challenge in these approaches is modeling and capturing the hierarchical relationships between terms, which is essential for effectively representing and understanding the semantic context of terms. This paper proposes a new approach to information retrieval based on Hierarchical Dirichlet Trees (HDTs) that captures the hierarchy between terms in a probabilistic framework. Our proposed model builds upon existing probabilistic modeling techniques by incorporating treelike structures to represent the relationships between terms, enabling the integration of semantic context and term hierarchies into the information retrieval process. The tree-based representation of terms allows our model to capture a broader range of relationships between terms, facilitating retrieval based not only on specific query terms but also their semantics. This is highly beneficial as relevant documents may contain terms other than those specified in the query but still be related semantically. By adopting a hierarchical structure for capturing term relationships, our model converges with the effect of inverse document frequency (IDF) which intuitively captures term significance by considering only those terms that appear across a high proportion of the documents while skipping those whose document coverage is limited although may have high frequency in relatively few documents. With its principled probabilistic framework and hierarchical tree structure, our HDT model enables a more sophisticated representation of term relationships, ultimately leading to improved retrieval accuracy by considering multiple query and term relationships simultaneously. This paper outlines our proposed model, explores its statistical properties, and demonstrates its efficacy in information retrieval experiments. The encouraging results show that HDTs offer substantial improvements over traditional baselines, ensuring that the hierarchical Dirichlet tree will become a powerful tool for information retrieval tasks. One key advantage of our model over previous approaches lies in its flexibility to incorporate various tree relationships and structure, allowing users to easily adapt it to different domains or collections. Moreover, our probabilistic formulation of HDTs empowers our model to naturally alleviate a fundamental problem of data sparsity commonly faced in information retrieval by borrowing strength across related terms and relationships.

Dialogue structure analysis is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), which refers to the process of identifying and segmenting a dialogue into coherent and meaningful components, such as utterances, turns, and topics. It plays a crucial role in various applications, including dialogue summarization, intent recognition, and human-computer interaction. Traditional approaches to dialogue structure analysis often rely on manually crafted rules or lexicons, which can be time-consuming, expensive, and do not generalize well to different domains or contexts. Furthermore, these methods typically require a large amount of labeled data to train, which is not always available. Recent advancements in data-driven methods have led to the development of machine learning models that can learn to identify dialogue structures without explicit programming or hand-crafted rules. Among these models, neural network-based approaches have shown impressive performance in various NLP tasks. However, most existing neural network models for dialogue structure analysis are designed for supervised learning, which require a large amount of labeled data to train. This limitation hampers their applicability to scenarios where labeled data is scarce or impossible to obtain. Our goal in this paper is to fill this gap by developing an unsupervised learning model that can identify dialogue structures without any labeled data. To address this problem, we propose a novel unsupervised learning model, called the hidden softmax sequence model (HSSM), based on a Boltzmann machine. The HSSM is designed to capture the hierarchical and sequential nature of dialogue structures by employing multiple types of hidden units. Specifically, our model has three types of hidden units: softmax units, which represent the latent states of utterances; binary units, which represent the latent topics specified by dialogues; and a global general topic unit, which represents the shared topic across the whole dialogue corpus. Moreover, the HSSM includes extra connections between adjacent hidden softmax units to model the dependency between the latent states of adjacent utterances. Our model offers several advantages over existing approaches. Firstly, the unsupervised learning capability of HSSM eliminates the need for manually labeled data, making it suitable for scenarios where labeled data is rare or difficult to obtain. Secondly, the hierarchical structure of our model allows it to capture the nested relationship between different dialogue components, such as utterances and topics. Finally, the probabilistic nature of our model enables it to model the uncertainty and variability inherent in human dialogue. In this paper, we evaluate the performance of the HSSM on two large-scale dialogue corpora: Twitter-Posts and Air-Ticket-Booking.

Dependency parsing is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), with applications in syntax-based machine translation, information extraction, and text summarization (Nivre, 2008; Carreras et al., 2010). Traditional dependency parsing methods typically rely on manually designed features and annotated data to induce a dependency grammar from a given corpus (Collins, 1996; Cooper et al., 2003). However, annotating corpora with dependency structures is a time-consuming and expensive process. Unsupervised dependency parsing, on the other hand, aims to learn a dependency grammar from text annotated with only part-of-speech (POS) tags, which can be obtained more easily (Ney et al., 2010; Li et al., 2014). A number of features and inductive biases have been proposed to incorporate prior knowledge into unsupervised dependency parsing. For instance, the use of manually designed features capturing the correlations between POS tags (Matsubara et al., 2014; Li et al., 2017) and the incorporation of special prior distributions to encode such information (Joshi et al., 2012) have been proposed. However, these approaches often require significant feature engineering effort and may not be easily transferable to new languages or domains. Furthermore, some of these approaches may also rely on pre-defined POS tag relationships, which can be biased towards particular linguistic patterns. Recent advances in neural networks have shown promise for unsupervised dependency parsing by learning dense and distributed representations of words and POS tags (Collobert et al., 2011; Socher et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2016). However, these approaches typically rely on annotated data and may not effectively capture the correlations between POS tags. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to unsupervised neural dependency parsing that leverages the power of distributed representations to predict grammar rule probabilities. Our model learns a distributed representation of POS tags from unlabeled text and uses this representation to predict the probability of a given grammar rule. This approach has several advantages over previous methods. Firstly, it can effectively capture the correlations between POS tags without requiring manual feature engineering. Secondly, it can be easily adapted to different languages and domains without relying on pre-defined POS tag relationships. Our experiments show that our approach outperforms previous methods utilizing POS correlations and is competitive with recent state-of-the-art approaches on nine different languages. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. We first introduce our unsupervised neural dependency parsing model and discuss the key components of the architecture.

The quality of web search can significantly vary across languages, even when searching for the same information need. This variation is due to several factors, including differences in indexing, relevance assessment, and ranking algorithms, which can lead to dissimilar search results across languages. While monolingual web search has received considerable attention in the past few years, bilingual web search (i.e., search that takes into account information from more than one language) has been somewhat underexplored. As a result, monolingual ranking functions that work well for a particular language may not work as well for other languages. To address this issue, we propose to exploit the variation in quality of web search across languages by learning a ranking function on bilingual queries. In particular, a bilingual query is a query that appears in query logs for two languages, but represents equivalent search interests. We assume that a given bilingual query, along with the corresponding monolingual query logs and monolingual ranking functions for each language, can be used to generate a ranking on pairs of documents, one from each language. Our key insight is that, for each pair of documents, we can learn features that capture their similarity or differences across languages, which can help improve the ranking of documents in a monolingual query. For example, a document in English and a document in Chinese may be highly relevant for a bilingual query, even if they have different keywords or topics. In this case, we can use bilingual features, such as language similarity or language-specific relevance models, to learn a ranking function that captures the relevance of the document pair across languages. We propose to learn a linear ranking function that exploits bilingual features on pairs of documents, as well as standard monolingual features. In addition, we show how to reconstruct a monolingual ranking function from a learned bilingual ranking function, which can be useful in practice. We evaluate our proposed bilingual ranking technique on publicly available Chinese and English query logs and demonstrate that it leads to significant improvements over a state-of-the-art monolingual ranking algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to apply learning to ranking on bilingual queries, where the goal is to learn a ranking function that captures the relevance of documents across languages. We also believe that our work opens up new opportunities for bilingual web search, including the ability to leverage bilingual queries to improve the quality of monolingual web search, as well as the potential to develop more effective language-specific ranking functions.

Phrase-based Statistical Machine Translation (PBSMT) models (Koehn et al., 2007) have achieved state-of-the-art results in many applications, and they remain a cornerstone of the field. Despite their success, there is still room for improving their performance, particularly when faced with out-of-domain or low-resource language pairs. One group of approaches that has been applied to improve the performance of PBSMT systems involves incorporating additional information into the translation estimation process, thereby providing a more informed ranking of possible translations. For example, Word Alignment (Gale and Church, 1993), and its variants (Chen and Rogers, 2006), have been widely employed to improve the alignment between source and target words, and thereby, their translations. Moreover, translation lexicon updates (Hildebrand et al., 2003), with word-level information, have been used to update the translation probabilities. Nonetheless, and as in other machine learning tasks, incorporating domain-specific knowledge is highly effective. For instance, domain adaptation (Blitzer et al., 2007), and its various variants (Ben-Nmedian, 2011), is a popular approach to take advantage of linguistic characteristics relevant to the new domain. Recent work has also shown the efficiency of incorporating multiple aligned example sentences to guide the search of the decoder (Tu et al., 2010). Motivated by these facts, we propose an additional type of information that can boost the quality of translations, namely, paraphrases of phrases. In effect, we investigate to what extent the quality of a phrase can be improved by taking its paraphrases into account in the estimation process. This new approach is founded on two main intuitions: firstly, a paraphrase can often synthesize a missing information and thereby help build a more informed translation distribution for a given phrase; secondly, these paraphrases can stimulate a new set of possible translations for that phrase. Moreover, and it is worth noting that we will be benefiting from the availability of large collections of example sentences in all the languages, thereby allowing the generation of more trained sentence-to-translation pairs. Our proposal can thus be seen as a more careful integration of word alignment, translation lexicon, adaptation techniques, and domain-specific information to our goal. In essence, the intention behind our proposal fits well with a rather active research area in machine translation, where attention has been placed in the use of non-parallel data to improve existing translation systems (e.g (Luo et al., 2014);(Rico, 2014),(Fung, 2009)). Some of them make use of manually constructed example sentences, such as translation memory, in order to guide the selection of appropriate translations, while others search on the web for relevant texts that may provide examples to enhance the translation

Document similarity is a fundamental problem in many areas of Natural Language Processing (NLP), particularly in information retrieval, clustering, and topic modeling. The nowadays most widely used and effective method to evaluate the similarity between text documents is based on the Bag-of-Words (BoW) representation, which represents each document as a vector of word frequencies. While BoW-based methods have been successful in many applications, they neglect the crucial relationships between words, such as semantic relationships like synonyms, antonyms, and hyponyms, which can be very informative for document similarity tasks. The dominance of word co-occurrence in the BoW representation may also lead to many irrelevant or unintended words being included as features, reducing the representation's effectiveness. Moreover, BoW representations do not take into account the structure and organization of the text, an important aspect of document meanings that may provide valuable information for document similarity tasks. To address these limitations, and build upon the benefits of graph-based models in capturing semantic relationships and structural patterns, we have developed a novel graph kernel for document similarity based on the shortest-path graph kernel. Our approach treats each document as a graph-of-words, where each word is a node, and the edges between the nodes capture the various relationships between the words in the text. Specifically, to construct the graph of-words for a given document, we can extract the stopwords and common words, such as pronouns, conjunctions, etc., from the training text and define them as nodes in the graph. For instance, we can use part-of-speech (POS) tagging and named entity recognition (NER) outputs as features to identify relevant entities and concepts in the text. To capture the relationships between these entities, we use edges that represent synsets (synonym sets), hyponyms, ontological relationships, collocations, or simply word co-occurrences. With this graph-of-words representation, we can use shortest-path graph kernels to compute the similarity between two documents. The histogram kernel and R-convolution kernel are popular choices for graph kernels for document classification. The key point in these kernels is computing the number of walks (or paths) between node pairs, which can capture higher-order relationships between words in the text. However, they may lead to high computational costs. On the other hand, the shortest-path graph kernel (SPGK), calculates the number of paths of a fixed length between two nodes (or words), which makes it more efficient for computing large-scale text graphs.

Human-computer conversation systems have been a hot research topic in the natural language processing (NLP) community for several years now. The rising popularity of virtual assistants like Siri, Alexa, and Google Assistant has fueled the need for more sophisticated and realistic conversation models. As users interact with these systems, they often expect meaningful and informative responses that demonstrate a deeper understanding of their queries. However, existing conversation systems based on the standard Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq) model through neural networks tend to fall short in this regard. While these systems can generate coherent and grammatically correct responses, they are often plagued by the problem of triviality – delivering responses that lack substance and fail to provide adequate information to the users. This is particularly evident when generating replies to complex or depth-demanding questions, where users expect the system to provide insightful and detailed answers. There are several reasons why the standard Seq2Seq model struggles with this task. Firstly, the model is primarily designed to learn the statistical patterns and dependencies between input and output sequences, often neglecting the underlying meaning and context of the conversation. Secondly, the model typically relies on a single, fixed set of input features, which may not be sufficient to fully capture the nuances and subtleties of human language. Finally, the model's design often prioritizes efficiency and ease of training over the quality of the generated responses, leading to shallow and uninformative outputs. In this paper, we aim to address these limitations and propose an implicit content-introducing method that incorporates additional information into the Seq2Seq model in a flexible and effective way. Our core contribution is the development of a hierarchical gated fusion unit, which seamlessly integrates general decoding and auxiliary cue word information to generate more meaningful and informative replies. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through thorough experiments on real-life conversation data, showcasing significant improvements in terms of both automatic metrics (BLEU scores) and human evaluation. Our results have significant implications for the development of advanced conversation systems that prioritize user engagement and satisfaction. By facilitating the incorporation of additional context and information, our method empowers conversation systems to provide more insightful and valuable responses, ultimately enhancing the overall user experience. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, we provide a detailed overview of the Seq2Seq model and its limitations in generating meaningful responses. We then introduce our proposed hierarchical gated fusion unit in Section 3, explaining how it integrates general decoding and auxiliary cue word information.

Visual question answering (VQA) is a challenging problem that requires both high-level computer vision skills and deep understanding of the questions being asked (Mnih et al., 2014; Malinowski et al., 2015). One extension of VQA is cross-lingual VQA, in which the questions asked are written in a different language than that of the images. This is related to work on zero-shot and few-shot learning (Koch et al., 2015), but goes further in leveraging language models to interpret visual scenes. The success of VQA has been due in part to the availability of several data sets for the English language, such as the VQA (Antol et al., 2015) and CLEVR (Johnson et al., 2017) datasets. However, these datasets have been found wanting for small language populations by Xia et al. (Xia et al., 2018), who found that directly converting the English language model to another language typically results in a poor transfer of knowledge. For example, in Chinese and Japanese, the syntax is more flexible, and the nuances of the language can be vastly different, such that directly applying English-based models has not been effective (Shneiderman et al., 2018). These factors point to the need for developing bilingual language datasets in addition to English, as well as cross-lingual methods that can leverage the power of both languages. The key point here is that these improvements come from focusing on transfer within the visual aspects of the task, rather than native language production. Word segmentation is a critical aspect of language acquisition, as it provides the foundation for building a vocabulary and understanding the structure of a language (Christophe et al., 2003;Cutler et al., 2002;Gros-Louis et al., 2005). Despite its importance, the factors that influence word segmentation are not well understood (Marcus et al., 1999). Studies of computational models of language acquisition provide one way to address this question, by providing a controlled environment in which to test various hypotheses about word segmentation. Computational models of language acquisition, such as Bayesian Word Segmentation (BWS), use data from child language corpora to build models of how children might segment words using different linguistic cues (Goldwater et al., 2003). Studies of these models can shed light on how children acquire language (Goldwater et al., 2006) and have implications for the development of language teaching methods. A key parameter of Bayesian Word Segmentation is the input size: how much audio and/or transcribed data are used by the model in making predictions about word segmentation. This parameter is critical, as it determines the amount of information available to the model for making those predictions. Yet, surprisingly, we know little about the relationship between input size and word segmentation performance (Marcus et al., 1999). Current available corpora for word segmentation studies, such as the CVST (Gros-Louis et al., 2006), are often not well-suited to the question of how input size affects word segmentation performance. One of the CVST limitations is the large variability in infant vocalizations, age variability in studied children and the high variability across different datasets. Because these factors can affect modeling performance, it is difficult to determine what factors are driving observed effects. Generating and following natural language instructions for complex sequential tasks represents a fundamental challenge in artificial intelligence and natural language processing. A key challenge in this area is that instructions often require the listener to carry out a sequence of actions, where each action relies on the successful outcome of the previous one. Taking a simple example, consider the instruction "Lift the heavy box, then carry it to the table, and place the object on top." In this case, the listener must unpack the potential sequential actions contained in the instruction and perform them in the correct order. Recent studies have highlighted the importance of understanding language processes and incorporating pragmatic reasoning to improve the generation and interpretation of instructions (Bisk et al., 2016). Unlike most natural language tasks, which are typically scoped to isolated, individual actions or objects, complex instructions often rely on an intricate understanding of context and the interplay between multiple actions, objects, and participants. A key challenge for natural language models that generate instructions is that it is critical to anticipate how the listener will interpret and act upon the generated instructions. For a pragmatic speaker model, the objective is to reason about why speakers produce specific instructions for a given task. This involves understanding the linguistic and extralinguistic factors that influence speaker choices, such as prior knowledge of the listener's psychology, ability, and context. To represent the pragmatic speaker, we can modify the listener model to simulate the interpretation of candidate descriptions. This thought experiment is useful for developing a speaker model that takes into consideration how its intended listeners are likely to interpret the speaker's output. At the same time, developing a pragmatic listener model enables us to simulate how listeners would process the speaker's output. Our extension to tasks with sequential structure involves processing a sequence of instructions that describe the performance of a sequence of actions. Our key contribution is the extension of these models, both listener and speaker, to sequential tasks. This involved developing a set of architectural modifications to handle the sequential structure of complex tasks and designing evaluation protocols to assess the benefits of pragmatic inference. In our main evaluations, we show that pragmatic inference significantly improves listener performance (correctly interpreting human instructions) and speaker performance (correctly generating instructions interpreted by humans) in diverse settings. In order to enable the listener model to process the sequential structure of complex instructions, we used a hierarchical neural architecture that combines the strengths of sequence-to-sequence models with the ability to compose more general policies for sequential action selection.

parses are a fundamental concept in NLP, where a parse tree allows us to break down a sentence into its constituent parts and express the relationships between them. Probabilistic context-free grammars (PCFGs) are a popular type of formal grammar that has been widely used for parsing tasks. A PCFG is a particular type of grammar in which each rule has an associated probability. This allows us to generate parse trees and estimate the probability of each tree. The PCFG model is widely used in NLP tasks such as parsing, machine translation, and language modeling because it allows us to capture hierarchical structure in the data. However, the estimation of PCFG parameters can be difficult due to the presence of latent variables, such as the correct parse trees. The standard approach to estimating PCFG parameters is through the use of an Expectation Maximization (EM) algorithm. The EM algorithm consists of two steps: an Expectation step and a Maximization step. In the Expectation step, we compute the expected log-likelihood of the data given the current model parameters and in the maximization step, we update the model parameters to maximize the expected log-likelihood. The EM algorithm does not converge to the global optimum, especially for large and complex models like PCFGs. A major limitation to the successful deployment of PCFGs is the difficulty in reliably estimating the parameters of the grammar given a potentially noisy dataset. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in developing PCFGs that can handle latent variables while providing guarantees on the quality of the learned model. However, developing efficient and computationally feasible learning algorithms for these models remains a significant challenge. In this paper, we introduce a new learning algorithm for latent-variable PCFGs that enjoys provable guarantees. Our algorithm applies a matrix-decomposition algorithm to co-occurrence matrices estimated from a set of parse trees. This step provides a set of distributions that approximate the probability distribution of a single tree and that have an intuitive graphical interpretation. The algorithm then applies a convex optimization algorithm to the output from this step. The main idea behind our approach is to factor the full PCFG probability distribution into two parts: one that depends on the latent variables and can be learned from the decomposition, and one that is specific to the PCFG model and can be learned through standard convex optimization. Our provably correct learning algorithm is based on a tractable EM optimization algorithm applied to a convex objective derived from the training data combined with the output from the matrix decomposition.

Generating high-quality text from a large set of structured data is a vital problem in many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. In recent years, neural network-based models have shown remarkable success in various text generation tasks, such as machine translation, text summarization, and question answering. However, most state-of-the-art models are designed for generating text from scratch or use a fixed vocabulary, making them limited in their ability to scale to large, complex domains. The challenge is particularly acute in domains like biography generation, where a vast amount of structured data is readily available but requires a nuanced understanding of language and meaning to produce coherent and informative text. The traditional approach to concept-to-text generation involves using templates or specialized language generation systems that require extensive hand-tuning and engineering expertise. In this paper, we propose a novel neural model for concept-to-text generation that can scale to large domains, leveraging the strengths of both neural networks and structured data. Our model is built on top of conditional neural language models for text generation, which have been shown to excel in various text generation tasks. However, to deal with the large vocabulary and structured data in the biography domain, we extend these models to incorporate two key innovations. First, we introduce a mixed vocabulary approach, where the model can select from a fixed vocabulary and copy certain words from the input database to the generated output sentence. This allows the model to capture domain-specific terminology and concepts while also generating text that is grammatically correct and fluently written. Second, we propose a data-aware word embedding approach, where the model can embed words differently depending on the data fields in which they occur. This enables the model to capture the nuances of language and meaning in the biography domain, where words may have different connotations and implications depending on the context in which they are used. To evaluate our model, we create a new dataset of biographies from Wikipedia, which contains over 700k samples and a vocabulary of 400k words. This dataset is an order of magnitude larger than existing resources, making it an ideal testbed for our model. We compare our model to a Templated Kneser-Ney (TKN) language model, which is a state-of-the-art model for generating text from templates. Our results show that our neural model significantly outperforms the TKN model by nearly 15 BLEU points, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach in scaling to large domains and generating high-quality text from structured data.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have emerged as a vital class of models for sequence modeling in recent years (Rumelhart et al., 1986). Among several variations of RNNs, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks have proven particularly successful in addressing the vanishing gradient problem that affects standard RNNs (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997). LSTMs work by coupling peephole connections within cells to create a gate-controlled feedback loop (Gers et al., 1999). By doing so, LSTMs are able to naturally and data-efficiently learn when to remember (engrave a piece of information) and when to forget (let a piece of information fade away) certain aspects of the input sequence. LSTMs have successfully been applied to tasks such as speech recognition (Graves et al., 2006), natural language processing (Bengio et al., 2003), and time-series prediction, which typically require more complex temporal dependencies than a simple linear chain can model. However, even more complex temporal phenomena can arise naturally from the interactions within sentence structure, governing linguistic phenomena relevant for various tasks, especially for linguistic meaning notwithstanding word order. Unfortunately, these tree-like structures have not been explicitly incorporated into LSTMs, which remain structured as straight chains. While RNNs of this form may learn impressive representations of linear sequence data such as text and speech, such representations lack the internal hierarchical relations which play an essential part in deeply grounded understanding. This paper presents a new extension of LSTMs called the Tree-LSTM, in which nodes in the network are arranged in a tree structure-i.e., a directed acyclic graph (DAG)-that mirrors the structure of natural language ontologies (Bruijn, 1949). We further argue that tree-like recurrent networks could naturally integrate the available sequence information that is inherent in most language and lead to an even further improvement of the representations arrived at. Broadly, to model tree structures, for each node we are trained with information from all its predecessors. This makes full use of the unique relationships between tree nodes that the usual RNN can use only in chains. Thus, Tree-LSTMs can serve to generate more complete and meaningful representations than traditional sequence models and this this yields the cognition-area quickest solution which several difficult NLP problems prompt. Several variations of the Tree-LSTM will be introduced alongside evaluations of its performance based on diverse datasets. By refining performance through modifications, we can complete a theoretical framework of how the general recurrent architecture falls into large distinctions.

Dogmatism is a personality trait that is characterized by a rigid and unyielding attitude to one's own beliefs and opinions. In everyday life, dogmatic individuals tend to be resistant to changing their views, and may use coercive tactics to impose their own opinions on others. Despite the significant impact of dogmatism on human relationships and collective group behavior, there has been relatively little research into the expression of dogmatic behavior on social media platforms. One promising venue for exploring the manifestation of dogmatism is the analysis of online conversation, particularly in interactive forums where disagreement is a common occurrence. Reddit, a popular internet forum for sharing and discussing content, offers an appealing setting for studying dogmatism in a naturalistic environment. A vast array of topics and sub-communities exist within Reddit, which presents the opportunity to analyze dogmatic behavior across a broad spectrum of domains and contexts. In this study, we aim to identify and model dogmatic behavior in social media by examining both linguistic and behavioral features. Our investigation begins by operationalizing key aspects of dogmatism described in existing psychology theories, such as over-confidence (Festinger, 1957), the tendency to reject contradictory information (Kunda, 1990), and a relative lack of openness to experience (Rokeach, 1960). To develop our statistical model, we utilize a large corpus of Reddit posts, covering a diverse range of conversational topics and collected via paid crowdsourcing, and operationalize dogmatism by coding the posts for the aforementioned features. Previous research suggests that dogmatism can manifest in distinct linguistic styles, such as the use of absolute language, emotive language, and a focus on assertive argumentation (Douglas, 1985). In addition, studies have identified behavioral patterns associated with dogmatic individuals, like their tendency to reject contradictory information, impose their own views on others, and show increased cognitive dissonance (Festinger, 1957). Our analysis reveals that these predicted linguistic and behavioral features indeed have significant predictive power for identifying dogmatic comments. Moreover, we discover new signals of dogmatism, such as a reluctance to signal cognitive processes, like imagination or creativity. By applying our model to a large-scale evaluation on millions of other Reddit posts, we find that dogmatic behavior appears to be a stable personality trait present across multiple domains and contexts. Our results suggest that individuals who frequently engage in dogmatic comments tend to display amplified dogmatic tendencies in their subsequent posts, indicating a positive feedback loop where dogmatic behavior reinforces itself.
