Geographic Information Systems (GIS) are widely used across a variety of fields, from urban planning and environmental analysis to navigation and search and rescue operations. However, they are often difficult to use for those without technical expertise, as they typically require a high degree of spatial literacy and familiarity with specialized query languages (e.g. SQL). In an effort to improve the accessibility and usability of GIS, several groups have proposed developing interfaces that allow users to query Geographic Information Systems using natural language (NL), as opposed to more traditional query methods such as point-and-click interfaces or text-based commands. Despite these efforts, there are still significant challenges to be addressed in the development of NL interfaces for GIS. One major challenge is building an accurate model of the mapping from natural language to geographic queries, often called "semantic mapping". Another challenge is designing an interface that allows users to express a wide range of queries, including complex or uncertain ones, in natural language. A key element of an NL interface for GIS is a "semantic parser". A semantic parser is a computational model that can analyze a natural language query and, based on domain knowledge, infer the specific query being referred to (i.e. the image or "logical form" that the query expresses). By converting a natural language query into a query that can be executed by a GIS, a semantic parser can provide users with a powerful new way to access and interact with geographic data. However, the development of accurate semantic parsers for GIS and, more generally, for NL databases is a difficult task. It requires large amounts of annotated data, models that can accurately capture the complex relationships between geographic entities, and methods that can adapt to the inherent uncertainties of natural language. One way to address these challenges is to use machine learning techniques, which can learn to represent and reason with complex data without hand-defined models. In this work, we make three major contributions: (1) the first large-scale corpus of natural language queries paired with machine-readable formulae for querying the OpenStreetMap (OSM) database, (2) an accurate semantic parser for the OSM database that allows users to query the database using natural language (and see their query on an interactive map), and (3) use of response-based learning on parser feedback to adapt a statistical machine translation system for multilingual database access to OSM.

Deep learning models, particularly those based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have achieved impressive results in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. 2 Convolutional neural networks have proven to be highly effective in NLP tasks such as text classification, sentiment analysis, and machine translation. 3 However, traditional CNNs process input data sequentially, where each position is processed independently of the others. 4 While this has been effective for image data, where a sequential processing order is implied, it does not capture certain complexities of text data. The success of CNNs in NLP tasks often relies on the choice of data preprocessing steps, such as tokenization and feature extraction, that filter out much of the locality and context from text data. The word embeddings used in most NLP tasks map words to a similar space, so they are more alike than they are different, ignore the nuances of the word, and disregard the word's context 5. However, for many NLP tasks, such as text classification and sentiment analysis, it is essential to consider the sequential and contextual nature of the input data (e.g., words). Inspired by the tensor-based methods, such as tensorspace and high-order tensor processing (HOTREP), used in NLP, 6 we propose a tensor-based approach for capturing word interactions in a differentiable manner. We represent word sequence data as a set of low-rank tensors where each tensor captures the interaction between words, with the goal of reducing the dimensionality while preserving the essential information contained in the input space. We define a convolution operation on these tensors, such that the convolution operation can be viewed as a series of single-channel kernels applied to the tensor. This tensor-enhanced convolution operation not only effectively captures the contextual information and non-local interactions between words but also enables the model to capture patterns in the data that may not be visible to a single word embedding. Additionally, we enable the model to capture non-consecutive patterns by considering the histogram kernel and soft- V score for pattern weighting. The resulting tensor-enhanced convolution operation requires only a constant number of operations per element and can thus be computed efficiently by dynamic programming. As a result, we can efficiently use large-scale word embeddings as input to our model while avoiding the computational bottlenecks associated with naive concatenation of word embeddings. We present the results of evaluations of our model on standard sentiment classification and news categorization tasks, where the proposed convolution leads to state-of-theart performance based on both metrics of accuracy and training speed.

Social media platforms have revolutionized the way people communicate with each other. The informal nature of these texts, characterized by the use of slang, abbreviations, and inconsistencies in spelling, poses significant challenges for natural language processing (NLP) tools. A crucial step in bridging this gap is text normalization, which involves restoring non-standard words to their canonical forms. Text normalization enables the effective processing of social media texts, crucial for tasks such as sentiment analysis, topic modeling, and information retrieval. In this paper, we propose a novel, graph-based approach to text normalization that leverages not only lexical features but also contextual and grammatical data. We approach social media text normalization as a problem of discovering meaningful patterns in an inherently noisy and variable environment. Traditional normalization methods rely heavily on manually constructed lists of canonical forms and rely primarily on surface-level similarity metrics between word forms. While these approaches show promise, they often struggle with normalization of words with multiple correct or acceptable forms. Inspired by the vast linguistic and contextual knowledge embedded in large social media datasets, we propose an unsupervised methodology that complements existing lexical features with contextual and grammatical patterns learned from a comprehensive graph. The word association graph, which forms the core of our approach, is constructed from a large unlabeled social media corpus. Each word is associated with a set of neighboring words, which in turn are related by their relative positions in the text and their part-of-speech (POS) tags. By examining and analyzing the graph structure, we leverage the collective knowledge of contextual usage to normalize non-standard words. Tree transducers are a type of formal model used to capture the transformation of tree structures in various domains such as natural language processing (NLP) and database applications. They consist of a set of rules where each rule corresponds to a labeled tree function, defining a transformation from a tree to another tree. In NLP, tree transducers are particularly useful for tasks such as linguistic analysis, sentiment analysis, and question answering, where tree structures provide rich information about the hierarchical organization of linguistic phenomena. However, one major issue in utilizing tree transducers is the difficulty of obtaining a sufficient number of high-quality training examples to induce the grammar of the transducer. Word-alignment (Galley et al., 2004), one common approach to inducing a transducer grammar, hinges on establishing a one-to-one correspondence between elements in an aligned source tree and their counterparts in a target tree by aligning the subtrees if they are isomorphic. Understanding the nuances of human language and common sense is an essential component of building a computer system that can effectively communicate and respond to natural language inputs. Despite advances in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, understanding casual and correlational relationships between events remains a challenging problem in the field of deep language understanding. This issue is not only an obstacle to building competent conversational systems but also a prerequisite for achieving more sophisticated NLP tasks, such as question answering, text summarization, and text generation. Script knowledge, which includes causal, temporal, and spatial relationships between events, is a fundamental aspect of understanding commonsense stories. Current data-driven NLP approaches often rely on large-scale datasets annotated with intricate relational information. However, previous research has shown that even the most comprehensive datasets may struggle to capture the depth and complexity of human common sense (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005; Li et al., 2016). For instance, co-occurrence of words or events in a large corpus is not necessarily a reliable indicator of causality, as evidenced in various studies on script knowledge and causal inference (Fritz and Ornstein, 1995; Moses, 2010). One major challenge in evaluating the quality of a system's common sense understanding is the lack of proper evaluation benchmarks and methodologies. This void often stems from our incomplete understanding of the underlying relationships between events, as well as the lack of well-annotated datasets that capture the breadth and depth of human common sense. To address these limitations, this paper presents a novel framework for assessing story understanding and script learning through the Story Cloze Test. The Story Cloze Test requires a system to choose the correct ending to a four-sentence story from a set of options, effectively measuring the system's ability to reason about causal and temporal relationships between events. We introduce a new corpus of 50k five-sentence commonsense stories, ROCStories, to enable this evaluation. ROCStories is a unique dataset in that it captures a rich set of causal and temporal commonsense relations, simulating everyday life scenarios, whereas maintaining high-quality standards for story coherence and integrity. This corpus offers not only an evaluation framework for story understanding but also a resource for training models on various NLP tasks, such as story generation and script learning. Our experimental results demonstrate that a range of baselines and state-of-the-art models based on shallow language understanding struggle to achieve a high score on the Story Cloze Test, underscoring the challenges of achieving deeper language understanding in this domain.

Dialogue analysis is a prominent research area that aims to understand the structure and dynamics of natural language interactions among humans. A fundamental challenge in dialogue analysis is measuring and modeling various aspects of dialogue quality, such as cooperation, coordination, and understanding. One essential aspect of cooperative dialogue is the exchange of appropriate and relevant information, which requires adhering to conventions and group norms. Deviation from these norms, or non-cooperation, can significantly affect the quality and outcome of the dialogue. Measuring non-cooperation is essential for understanding various aspects of dialogue, such as identifying problematic communication styles, detecting deception, and evaluating the performance of dialogue systems. Previous work on non-cooperation has relied on human evaluation, relying on annotators to assess the degree of cooperation by manually scoring the dialogue based on certain criteria. However, this method is time-consuming, costly, and often subjective. Moreover, previous research has mainly focused on modeling non-cooperation in terms of specific behaviors or actions that are considered non-cooperative, such as lying or dominating the conversation. In contrast to this categorical approach, we aim to develop a more nuanced and quantitative measure of non-cooperation by focusing on the extent to which dialogue participants deviate from relevant conversational conventions, such as the obligation to respond to a question or the obligation to ask for clarification when certain. To develop such a measure, we draw on insights from dialogue theory and pragmatics, which provide a framework for understanding the normative structure of dialogue and identifying the obligations that speakers have towards each other. Specifically, we rely on the theory of dialogue games (Ludwik Fleck, 1935;Martin Emil Krogh Jensen and Grønmo:2011), which describes dialogue as a strategic interaction between players who engage in a sequence of moves to achieve a common goal. A dialogue game is formally defined as a tuple consisting of players, moves, a scoring function, and a condition of winning. Moreover, dialogue games may include conversational norms and obligated moves that describe the duties and responsibilities of each participant in the conversation. By defining dialogue games as formal models of conversation rules and cooperative obligation fulfillment, we can systematically analyze the structure of a dialogue and identify instances of non-cooperation based on participants' deviations from these rules. In our paper, we present a novel method for measuring non-cooperation based on the concept of "dialogue games," where cooperation is seen as a normative concept based on obligatory dialogue moves.

Keyphrase generation is a crucial task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), which refers to automatically identifying a set of phrases that capture the main ideas and topics of a given text, such as a document or a paper. Keyphrases help readers quickly understand the content and context of a document, making the summarization process more efficient and effective. With the rapid growth of online content, automatic keyphrase generation has become increasingly important for Information Retrieval (IR), text classification, recommender systems, and other applications that require a concise representation of text content. Although conventional approaches to keyphrase generation have shown promising results, they often neglect the correlation among keyphrases, resulting in duplication and coverage issues. For instance, some existing methods select multiple identical keyphrases or fail to cover all important topics of a document, which reduces the effectiveness of keyphrase generation. Moreover, previous approaches often ignore the context and relation between keyphrases, leading to incompatible or irrelevant keyphrases, which may confuse readers or hamper further processing of the keyphrases. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel sequence-to-sequence architecture, named CorrRNN, specifically designed for keyphrase generation with correlation constraints. Building upon the recent advances in sequence-to-sequence learning and conditional random fields, CorrRNN effectively captures correlation among multiple keyphrases and leverages the context and relation between them. There are two key aspects of CorrRNN that capture correlation among keyphrases. Firstly, we introduce a coverage vector to monitor whether the word in the source document has been summarized by previous phrases. With this coverage vector, we can emphasize the importance of novel information and minimize the repetition of information that has already been captured by previous phrases. Secondly, we incorporate a forward coroutine mechanism that allows preceding phrases to be taken into account, effectively pruning duplicate phrases and preserving the coherence of the keyphrases. In the following sections, we provide a detailed description of CorrRNN and conduct extensive experiments to evaluate its performance on benchmark datasets in terms of both accuracy and diversity. The experimental results demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art method in capturing keyphrases that are accurate, diverse, and free from duplication. The evaluation also highlights the viability and sensitivity of CorrRNN to different architectural configurations and hyperparameters. Our findings suggest that incorporating correlation constraints in keyphrase generation can lead to substantial improvements in the quality and relevance of the generated keyphrases, which is of paramount importance for various downstream applications.

Inference in graphical models can be a computationally challenging task, particularly in large models with intricate structures. Traditional algorithms such as exact inference and Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling often suffer from scalability issues when dealing with complex models over large state spaces. A prominent approach to approximate inference is belief propagation (BP), which has been widely adopted in various fields including computer vision, speech recognition and natural language processing. However, loopy BP is computationally expensive and typically do not apply to multimodal distributions (Minka and Greiger, 2008). Recent years, variants of BP such as expectation propagation (EP) (Minka and Greiger, 2008) have been proposed to approximate inference, where projections of self-normalized messages onto a small exponential family of distributions are updated iteratively in BP steps. However, similar to loopy BP, general EP is not guaranteed to converge to the true distribution if the initial message and the family of the projection functions are arbitrary (Opper, 2001;Minka and Greiger, 2008). Moreover, in multimodal distributions, the ep is more computationally expensive to perform per iteration . In the context of graphical models, approximate inference typically proceed by sending messages along edges of the graph involving either approximate posterior distributions over a subset of the variables or the likelihood scores for the variables (Krishnan et al., 2017;Domke and Shahbaba, 2015). In this paper, we propose penalized expectation propagation (PEP), which improves the efficiency by adding a structured sparsity term to the message updates in expectation propagation, such that even if the original messages significantly vary throughout the iterations of PEP, the weighted sum is smooth. We demonstrate that structured sparsity greatly accelerates the initialization and convergence speed with maintained accuracy without going to numerical instabilities, given that we impose an appropriate form for the penalty term to act as a regularization on the simple messages. Conventional structured sparsity is typically used to histogram the highly weighted angles (Müller et al., 2006), which belongs to supervised learning (Greger, 2010). In our approach, different from previous work, we integrate structured sparsity directly into free energy formulation, then need to reoptimize only one of the parameters of a predetermined dominant direction, but with no further requirement of supervised learning. PEP is instantiated by choosing tractable message forms subject to structured-sparse distribution approximations. The term “structured sparsity precondition based free energy” denotes the modified free energy in this paper, where structured sparsity formulation only acts on the information of critical points.

Synchronous context-free grammars (SCFGs) have been widely used in natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning (ML) tasks. SCFGs provide a way to model the syntactic and semantic structures of language, making them a valuable tool for tasks such as machine translation, parsing, and language modeling. However, the group testing Knuth-Morris-Pratt (GHKM) parsing algorithm (Arnborg et al., 2006) underlying most SCFG decoding algorithms relies on the Chomsky Normal Form (CNF) (Chomsky, 1959) to ensure cubic time complexity. Estimating the class prevalence, defined as the proportion of a population belonging to a given class, is a fundamental problem in statistics and machine learning. In many applications, such as document categorization, the interest lies not only in classifying an individual document, but also in inferring the class distribution of the entire document collection. Previous work on prevalence estimation primarily relies on aggregating and adjusting discriminative individual classifiers (Goodman and Smyth, 2006;Hullermeier et al., 2008;Wolpert, 2006;Geweke, 2011) to produce point estimates. However, imperfect classifier accuracy, which is inherently uncertain, remains unaddressed in these approaches, thereby undermining their reliability and interpretability. In many scientific settings, robust and statistically valid inference calls for an explicit reflection of this uncertainty (Johnson, 2005). The key insight is that existing discriminative classifiers can be given a generative reinterpretation, enabling the estimation of the likelihood function for individual samples and, consequently, the derivation of the class prevalence through Bayesian inference. In particular, we demonstrate that a discriminative classifier can be converted into a generative model through simple mathematical transformations, which yield an explicit representation of the samplelikelihood function. By backtracking from the classification output to the underlying sample likelihood, we can leverage this generative interpretation to compute group-level prevalence and quantify the associated uncertainty via Bayesian inference (Gelman et al., 2013). Error correction is a critical component of language processing systems, particularly in applications involving non-native language speakers, such as machine translation and language learning tools. In these applications, the correction of grammatical and lexical errors, including preposition usage, is essential for producing fluent and accurate text. Despite the importance of preposition usage in natural language, existing correction approaches often treat all prepositions as equally likely corrections, regardless of the context. This can lead to suboptimal corrections, where the most appropriate preposition is not selected. For instance, when a non-native speaker writes "I go store to buy milk", the correct correction "I go to the store to buy milk" requires knowledge of the appropriate preposition usage in this context. A correct correction must take into account the specific syntactic and semantic features of the sentence, including the choice of preposition. In this paper, we focus on the task of generating candidate corrections for error correction in preposition usage made by non-native English speakers. We propose a novel approach, which generates candidate corrections by determining likely preposition confusions using an annotated corpus of non-native text. We show that restricting candidate sets to those that are observed in the non-native data significantly improves both the precision and the recall of correction compared to the standard approach that views all prepositions as possible candidates. Existing approaches to error correction in language processing rely heavily on machine learning and corpus-based methods. Machine learning models for error correction often use a predefined set of possible corrections, which can be based on a dictionary of words or a large corpus of text (He et al., 2018). However, such approaches have limitations. The predefined set of possible corrections may not contain the correct correction, leading to suboptimal results. Moreover, the similarity between the incorrectly written word and the possible corrections can be misleading, resulting in incorrect corrections being selected. In order to address these limitations, we draw inspiration from recent advances in active learning and meta-learning, and propose a novel method to generate candidate corrections based on likely preposition confusions. Our approach leverages an annotated corpus of non-native text to determine the most likely preposition confusions. We train a discriminative classifier on this corpus to predict the correct preposition usage given a specific sentence. By analyzing the confidence of the classifier, we can estimate the likelihood of each preposition confusion in the non-native text.

Coreference resolution is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), aiming to identify all occurrences of an entity or pronoun in a piece of text and relate them to their corresponding antecedent (or anaphor) (Chini et al., 2011). Despite the significant advances in recent years, coreference resolution remains a challenging task due to the complexities and nuances of human language. Recent work has highlighted the importance of explicitly identifying and filtering non-anaphoric mentions prior to coreference resolution, in order to significantly improve the performance of a coreference system (Lee et al., 2014; Clark and Gupta, 2016). These non-anaphoric mentions can arise from a variety of linguistic phenomena, such as nominalizations (e.g., "the team's victory"), prepositional phrases (e.g., "on the table"), and subordinate clauses (e.g., "while waiting for the bus"). A key challenge in anaphoricity determination is identifying these non-anaphoric mentions and distinguishing them from anaphoric mentions (i.e., pronouns or nominalizations that refer to an entity previously mentioned). An effective anaphoricity determination module can filter out the non-anaphoric mentions and help the coreference system focus on the relevant mentions to be resolved. Motivated by this, we present in this paper a novel approach to anaphoricity determination based on graph cuts. The core idea is to formalize anaphoricity determination as a labeling problem on a graph, where each mention (both pronominal and nominal) is a node and the edges between nodes represent the cognitive relationships between mentions. We then apply graph cut algorithms to minimize an energy function that captures the cost of labeling each node with anaphoricity and non-anaphoricity. Our proposed method, named GCAnaph, shows superiority over competing approaches in improving a learning-based coreference system on the ACE 2004 English and ACE 2005 Chinese data sets. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we discuss relevant work in coreference resolution and anaphoricity determination. In Section 3, we describe the graph-based formulation of anaphoricity determination. Section 4 presents the implementation of our proposed GCAnaph method. We experiment with both the ACE 2004 English and ACE 2005 Chinese data sets in Section 5. We conclude the paper with a summary of the main findings in Section 6. Throughout this paper, we use the terms "anaphor" and "anaphoricity" to refer to both pronouns and nominalizations that refer to previously mentioned entities. We assume familiarity with the basic concepts of coreference resolution and learning-based coreference systems (Lee et al., 2014).

Minimum Error Rate Training (MERT) is a popular method for optimizing the performance of machine translation (MT) systems by selecting parameter values that maximize performance on a given tuning set, typically measured by an automatic evaluation metric, such as BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002). MERT has been widely adopted in MT research and development due to its simplicity and effectiveness, particularly when the system will eventually be evaluated using the same metric. However, in real-world scenarios, most MT evaluations involve a human-based component, where human assessors evaluate the quality of translations against certain quality metrics or reference translations. This introduces a challenge in performing MERT with human-based metrics, as it requires involving human evaluators at the tuning stage, which is often impractical and expensive. Furthermore, MERT relies on a large number of candidate translations to select the optimal set of parameters, leading to the proliferation of redundant or similar candidate sentences during the tuning process. In this study, we investigate the feasibility of human-in-the-loop MERT and propose a novel approach to circumvent the need for human input at the tuning stage, while still utilizing human judgments to inform the evaluation metric. Our solution involves designing a reranking metric, referred to as RYPT (Ranking Yield Percentage Threshold), which takes human judgments into account, yet only requires human input to build a database that can be reused over and over again. In essence, RYPT combines the benefits of automatic evaluation metrics with the insights of human evaluators, providing a more accurate predictor of translation quality. This paper presents the following contributions: • We introduce the reranking metric RYPT and demonstrate its ability to account for human judgments while being scalable and efficient. • We analyze the diversity of candidate translations produced during MERT and show that redundancy can be harnessed to improve tuning efficiency and reduce testing overhead. • We illustrate the superiority of RYPT over BLEU as a predictor of translation quality, taking into account the relatively high cost and variability of human evaluation. We explore the applicability of RYPT to real-world applications and envision its potential as a more robust and cost-effective alternative to BLEU-based tuning methods. By incorporating human expertise into the training loop, we aim to boost the viability and reliability of machine translation systems in practical settings. By targeting a more holistic understanding of the translation process, we can improve the overall quality of MT systems and enable them to meet the demands of various stakeholders in the translation community.

Conventional maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) is widely used to train phrase-based translation models. Although effective in many cases, this approach has several limitations. Firstly, estimating the large number of translation probabilities required by these models can be computationally expensive and often results in models with sparse probability distributions. Secondly, the discrete representations of translation units, typically based on phrase pairs or n-gram phrases, can lead to over-smoothing and poor performance on low-frequency words. Finally, a major issue is the lack of sufficient training data, which typically restricts the model to consider a small amount of context. While some models attempt to enlarge the data size available for training, the MLE approach remains essentially the same. As an alternative to MLE, a number of recent studies have explored different estimation strategies and representations of the translation units. One such family of models is continuous space translation models, which estimate translation probabilities using a continuous representation of translation units in lieu of standard discrete representations. Our goal is to evaluate the effectiveness of continuous space models for machine translation, and to propose a framework in which these models can be effectively trained and used on top of a standard n-gram translation system. We believe that continuous space representations offer several advantages over conventional discrete representations. Firstly, they potentially reduce over-smoothingand facilitate the modeling of rare or out-of-vocabulary words. Secondly, they may alleviate the need for extensive data augmentation or artificial language corpora. To further boost the training efficiency and model capacity, we propose a multi-layer neural network architecture with a specially designed SOUL (Separate Output Units Layout) structure. The proposed network is designed to handle a large set of translation units by jointly computing the representations and the associated estimates. This supervised modeling enables our models to integrate context from a larger portion of the text and consider a wider range of related words in the output space, meeting the major demands for the low- to high-frequency words. The effectiveness of our proposed models is demonstrated in both small-scale and large-scale experiments on English-to-French machine translation, using BLEU scores for evaluation. By comparing our proposed approaches with those of existing models and language technology systems, we aim to demonstrate the applicability and promise of continuous space translation models with neural networks. In the following sections, we review related work, describe the continuous space translation models with a neural network architecture, present the implementation details, and report our experimental results.

Cross-lingual understanding and machine translation are two central objectives in natural language processing. However, while notably advances have been made in both areas, nowadays though it is relatively easy to produce highly accurate translations from one language to another, there still remains a significant problem of bridging the gap between languages. Current methods primarily rely on language-specific token embeddings, lexical substitution scores and linguistic/role tagging, which fall far short of human abilities to understand semantical translations of meaning. One intermediate objective is to improve bilingual text embeddings, and numerous approaches have been proposed to tackle this issue, including bilingual dictionary learning (Mikolov et al., 2013b; Meng et al., 2014) and self-training with parallel corpora (Klementiev et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2013). However, while effective, these methods suffer from the inherent limitation that if a word is out-of-vocabulary or there is not an in-domain parallel corpus, it is difficult to leverage shared linguistic information more effectively. To overcome these issues, a few approaches have been proposed more recently, such as additive bilingual word embeddings (Klementiev et al., 2012) and proto-lexicons (xian et al., 2020). Still these methods did not effectively transfer cross lingual knowledge in different sentences as they may overlook relationships between images, potentially resulting in lower performance in zero-shot cross-lingual image retrieval and semantic textual matching tasks. To leverage the power of images in this scenario, we propose a model based on deep partial canonical correlation analysis (PCCA), known for its age-old association with applicability in high-noise high-signal to noise ratio datasets. In addition, while the original PCCA finds linear projections of two views in order to maximize their canonical correlation conditioned on a shared third variable, we introduce a non-linear Deep PCCA (DPCCA) model, capable of finding complex relationships between an input vector from histogram's image features, a target vector in word embeddings and a bridge vector (image description given by sentence). DPCCA is computationally more efficient than prior image-to-text alignment models, since it only needs to differentiate between different representations in each iteration. Moreover, to our knowledge, we are the first to estimate DPCCA via stochastic iterative algorithm for this data. Our implementation leverages visual features for bilingual word embeddings, allowing PCCA and DPCCA to achieve state-of-the-art levels of cross-lingual word similarity and zero-shot performance through image-description retrieval, desipte the absence of any visual signal during test-time inference.

Temporal relation classification is a crucial task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), which involves determining the causal relationship between events and time expressions in a given text. There are several types of temporal relationships, including before (e.g., "The meeting finished before the party started"), after (e.g., "The meeting started after the coffee was served"), includes (e.g., "The summer includes June, July, and August"), during (e.g., "The construction project will take place during the next few months"), and overlap (e.g., "The meeting will overlap with the conference"). While there have been significant advancements in traditional temporal relation classification, the problem remains a challenging one, particularly when dealing with varying levels of contextual and temporal complexity. Existing approaches to temporal relation classification typically involve extensive feature engineering, which often involves manual extraction of linguistic and temporal features from the input text, followed by the application of machine learning algorithms to predict the correct temporal relation. However, these methods can be labor-intensive, and their effectiveness is often limited by the availability of large-scale annotated datasets. Moreover, the feature engineering process can be time-consuming and require significant domain expertise, making it difficult to generalize across different NLP applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach based on parse tree similarity that does not require extensive feature engineering. Our approach relies on a simple yet effective measure of parse tree similarity, which involves computing tree similarity values using a convolution kernel as input to a dependency parse tree. This approach has several advantages, including ease of implementation, low computational overhead, and robustness to varying levels of contextual and temporal complexity. Our results show that this approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art in temporal relation classification. To further improve classifier performance, we explored the feasibility of acquiring high-quality annotations through crowdsourcing. While crowdsourcing has been successfully applied to a variety of NLP tasks, the temporal relation classification task poses unique challenges due to its complexity and subtlety. However, our results demonstrate that high-quality annotations can indeed be crowdsourced from novice annotators, provided that the annotation task is carefully designed and optimized. One critical aspect of our crowdsourcing approach is the careful selection of annotation tasks to minimize the effort required for training data annotation. By leveraging the problem structure of temporal relation classification, we designed an annotation strategy that selectively acquires annotations on problem instances that are assessed as more difficult.

Low-resource neural machine translation (NMT) remains an open challenge in the field of natural language processing. Despite recent advancements in multilingual and unsupervised NMT, large amounts of data are required for training high-quality NMT systems. However, many languages lack sufficient parallel data, hindering the deployment of NMT systems for these languages. A promising approach to address this challenge is multi-source and multi-target NMT (Arivazhagan et al., 2019;Fan et al., 2019), which leverages pre-trained NMT systems to translate across related languages. Nevertheless, multi-source and multi-target data may not always be available. An alternative approach to handle the lack of data is self-supervised learning (Lample and Conneau, 2019;Gupta et al., 2020), which employs tasks such as back-translation, round-trip translation, or denoising autoencoders to generate synthetic parallel data for fine-tuning. Another promising direction is meta-learning for NMT (Hou et al., 2019;Aharoni and Goldberg, 2019), which aims to train the model to adapt quickly to new languages and unseen data distributions. Meta-learning algorithms, such as model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) (Finn et al., 2017), were originally designed for few-shot learning in computer vision. In this work, we adapt MAML to the task of low-resource NMT, leveraging its ability to learn to adapt quickly to new languages and unseen data distributions. We propose a novel extension of MAML, which we term meta-learning for NMT, and show that it significantly outperforms the multilingual, transfer learning based approach (Zoph et al., 2016) and enables us to train a competitive NMT system with only a fraction of training examples. Our work builds upon the recent introduction of universal lexical representations (Gu et al., 2018b) to handle the input-output mismatch across different languages. Entity linking is the task of identifying a specific content entity (e.g., a person, location, organization) mentioned in a piece of text and linking it to a corresponding entry in a knowledge base (KB) (Ratinov et al., 2011). It's an important step in many NLP applications, including information extraction, question answering, and text summarization. Entity linking can serve as a convenient gateway to encyclopedic information, greatly improving a web user's experience (Shen et al., 2012). Recent years have witnessed a significant surge of research interest in entity linking, driven by the advance of deep learning techniques and the availability of large scale annotated datasets. Early works typically cast entity linking as a classification problem, where the goal is to classify each mention of an entity as a specific entity (e.g., (Etzioni et al., 2008)). However, this problem is fundamentally different from typical classification problems. In classification, all instances are supposed to belong to one of the predefined classes; whereas in entity linking, there may not be a corresponding entry for an entity in the KB. Moreover, the entities in the KB that do belong to the relevant classes are often heavily unequal in quality and relevance, resulting in disorder in the truth values. These factors make it more suitable to consider entity linking as a ranking problem, where the goal is to rank entities in decreasing order of relevance for a given mention (McClosky et al., 2010]. Ranking models have been proven to be effective in dealing with the issues of imbalanced and disorder data in IR tasks, such as information retrieval. The goal of this paper is to present a learning to rank algorithm for entity linking. We aim to address the problems mentioned above in the previous classification based models. We propose a framework that formulates entity linking as a ranking task over candidate entities related to the current mention. The ranking model is trained to optimize a ranking loss function that encourages an entity to be ranked higher if it is indeed the target entity to be linked, thereby effectively utilizing the relationship information among the candidates when ranking. Experimental results on the TAC 2009 KBP Slot Filling dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework. We also conduct comparisons to existing methods and show that our ranking model achieves 18.5% improvement in terms of accuracy over classification models for those entities which have corresponding entries in the Knowledge Base.

Human-robot interaction (HRI) is a sector of research that involves the interaction between humans and robots. A key challenge in HRI is the design of usable and natural interfaces that enable humans to communicate effectively with robots. Dialogue systems, in particular, have been actively researched as they allow humans to directly interact with robots using language (Bisk et al., 2016). However, the usability of a dialogue system can have significant impacts on both the efficiency of the interaction and the user's overall experience with the system (Isbister et al., 2000). To ensure that a dialogue system is usable, it is essential to understand the key factors that affect a human's experience with the system. This requires identifying both objective and subjective measures of the system's quality. A number of objective measures of usability have been proposed (Holmes et al., 2011; Bloom et al., 2007), such as the efficiency of the interaction (e.g., the time it takes to complete a task, the number of turns required), the correctness of the interactions (e.g., whether the user receives correct information, the accuracy of the user input), and the engagement level (e.g., the user's participation level, the dialog length), among others. Subjective measures, on the other hand, can provide insight into the user's emotional experience with the dialogue system (Chellappa and Ghosal, 2005; Blanchard et al., 2012). User satisfaction, task completion, and ease of use are examples of subjective measures that have been used in HRI studies. In this paper, we present a study in which naïve subjects interacted with a human-robot dialogue system that enabled users to work together with a robot to build wooden construction toys. We describe a wide range of objective and subjective measures of the system's usability, including both positiveresults, such as efficient dialogue workflows, and negative results, such as long-turn interactions. To assess which aspects of the interaction had the greatest impact on the users' opinions of the system, we used a method based on the PARADISE evaluation framework (Walker et al., 1997) to derive a performance function from our data. We then examined the contributions of specific features of the interactions to user satisfaction. The contribution of this paper can be summarized as the following: we propose a human-robot dialogue system for building wooden construction toys that is able to work together with a human user, and assess both objective and subjective measures of the system's usability.

Phrase-based translation systems have been widely used in statistical machine translation (SMT) to model word reordering during translation. In typical state-of-the-art phrase-based systems, the reordering of phrases is determined by lexicalized reordering models, such as n-gram-based models or decision trees (Galley and Manning, 2008;Galley et al., 2006). However, these lexicalized reordering models have three significant drawbacks that limit their effectiveness. Firstly, they are heavily context insensitive because the reordering probabilities are computed using only the current phrase pair, without considering the context of previous phrase pairs. This makes them ineffectual when the translation context requires knowledge of previous phrases to appropriately reorder the new one. Moreover, lexicalized reordering models are plagued by reordering ambiguity (Galley et al., 2004), with multiple possible reorders of the phrases to achieve the same translation. This is because the word order of each phrase is directly converted into a reordering instruction without any consideration of the surrounding context. The third drawback of lexicalized reordering models is the sparsity of their parameter space, which leads to poor performace in some conditions, such as when relevant training data is limited or heavy-tailed. To address these drawbacks, Tomohide et al. proposed certain context- insensitive reordering model which filters sentences as sentence preprocessing phase. However, there are trade-off between filtering and translation because sentence filtering defeats the purpose of machine translation. Here, we explore a novel approach to address these issues and improve the effectiveness of phrase-based models. In this paper, we propose a neural reordering model that incorporates the words of both the current and previous phrase pairs into the reordering decision. We condition reordering probabilities on a rich representation of both the current and previous phrase pairs, allowing our model to effectively capture contextual information and reduce reordering ambiguity. Additionally, we adopt continuous vector space representation for phrase pairs and a single classifier for all phrase pairs to alleviate the data sparsity problem. By addressing these limitations, we show that our neural reordering model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art lexicalized reordering models on the NIST Chinese-English datasets. Our approach joins a growing line of work leveraging deep learning architecture to improve SMT. Deep learning has shown promising results in various NLP tasks and this research assess the ap-area of SMT by providing a novel way of reordering. Firstly, the vector space representation leads to more effective use of data based on diverse sourced corpora and can also ameliorate the permutations of data in BERT or Wordpiece type models.

Commonsense knowledge is a fundamental component of human intelligence, allowing individuals to make sound judgments and decisions in a wide range of situations. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in constructing and leveraging large-scale commonsense knowledge bases, such as ConceptNet (Speer and Havasi, 2012) and ATOMIC (Sap et al., 2019), to support a variety of natural language processing and human-computer interaction tasks (Chen et al., 2013). ConceptNet is an open multilingual lexical database that contains a vast array of concepts, relations, and language-dependent associations. It is particularly appealing because it contains many knowledge connections that are less frequent but no less important than those in existing resources. However, manually curating such a vast amount of knowledge and ensuring its accuracy and completeness remains a challenging task. We argue that a key challenge facing ConceptNet is the lack of a robust and scalable approach to automatically enriching it with new knowledge, while also ensuring its quality and coherence. In this paper, we frame this problem as one of knowledge base completion, focusing on the task of predicting missing relations between arbitrary phrases that are likely to hold true. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach based on neural network models for scoring these tuples. Knowledge base completion (KBC) has become a core problem in NLP, with applications including question answering, natural language inference, and entity disambiguation (Fan et al., 2019). Most prior work on KBC focuses on knowledge bases such as Freebase (Bollacker et al., 2008) and YAGO (Suchanek et al., 2007) that contain relationships between a fixed set of entities. However, the rel ationships in ConceptNet are much more diverse, involving phrases that represent both entities and relations, and furthermore, the number of possible entities and relationships is virtually unlimited. Moreover, because phrases may be structured hierarchically or composed from sub-phrases, the notion of "similarity" between phrases is not as simple as for traditional entities (Gaissmaier et al., 2009). In our work, we break the complexity of scoring arbitrary phrases free from the limitations of static entity sets by designing and evaluating novel neural architectures that are specifically tailored to handle the special characteristics of this data. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: 1. We reframe the knowledge base completion problem in the context of ConceptNet and introduce a challenging task of predicting missing relations between arbitrary phrases that are likely to hold true.

Representation learning is a critical component of many Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks, particularly text classification. Traditional text classification models largely rely on shallow feature engineering and usually ignore the semantic information embedded in the text, hinderingtheir performance on complex tasks. With the advent of deep learning, many deep neural models have been proposed to learn representations from raw text data. However, existing models suffer from several limitations. On the one hand, some models like Word2Vec (Le and Mikolov, 2014) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) mainly learn local semantic representations based on the co-occurrence of words in the document. However, these models ignore the global structure information of the document. On the other hand, many structure-based models like Recursive Neural Networks (RNNs) (Socher et al., 2011; dai et al., 2015) rely on the manually annotated or parsed input to capture the global structure information. However, these models have significant limitations: 1) they require a tremendous amount of annotated data, which is very expensive to obtain, and 2) the structured parsing results cannot capture the linguistic complexity of natural languages, such as heavy use of relative clauses and elliptical constructions. A major design goal for text representation learning models is to automatically capture both local semantic and global structure information. However, there are many challenges in achieving this goal because local semantics and global structure information are usually interdependent and relate to each other in sophisticated ways. For instance, long sentences with many verbs and prepositions provide more structure information than short sentences with little connection between words. Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have led to the development of more sophisticated language models that can capture the nuances of human language. Among these, joint language models that incorporate both lexical and syntactic information have shown significant improvements over their lexical-only counterparts [Sutskever et al., 2011;Merity et al., 2017]. However, the majority of these models rely on part-of-speech (POS) tags as the primary source of syntactic information. This simplification limits their ability to capture more fine-grained aspects of language structure, which are crucial for understanding and generating coherent sentences. To address this limitation, we present a scalable joint language model that is designed to utilize fine-grain syntactic tags, which can capture more detailed syntactic relationships and structures in the language. Fine-grain syntactic tags differ from conventional POS tags by providing a more granular view of the sentence structure, capturing phenomena such as negation, question formation, and clause dependencies. Our model, which we refer to as the Joint Language Model (JLM), combines the strengths of traditional n-gram models with the ability to perform more sophisticated syntactic analysis. Integrating fine-grain syntactic tags into a joint language model poses several challenges. Firstly, it requires a large and well-annotated dataset with fine-grain syntactic tags, which is a time-consuming and resource-intensive task. Secondly, dealing with a large number of tags can lead to the curse of dimensionality, making the model more prone to overfitting. Finally, the computational complexity of the model increases exponentially with the number of tags, making it computationally expensive to train and evaluate. To address these challenges, we propose a number of simplifications and techniques that can be used to scale the model to large tagsets and corpora. We simplify the task of annotation by using a relatively small set of fine-grain tags that do not require deep linguistic knowledge of the language but provide more structural information than POS tags. We also develop an efficient annotation scheme that can be easily adopted for new languages. To evaluate our model, we implement two fine-grain tagsets and compare the performance of our model using these tags with that of a traditional POS-based model and a recent state-of-the-art model that uses SuperARV tags. Our results show that the JLM achieves significant improvements over the baseline models in a speech recognition task, particularly when using fine-grain syntactic tags.

Sentiment analysis on product reviews has become increasingly important due to the huge rise of e-commerce and the fact that customers express their opinions in online forums nowadays. Most of the existing studies are based on the bag-of-words model and basic sentiment lexicons, which suffer from the following limitations: (1) The knowledge of hierarchical relationships of product attributes is not fully utilized; (2) Reviews or sentences mentioning several attributes associated with complicated sentiments are not dealt with very well. For example, A product review says "The design of the new iPhone 6 is really fancy and sleek, but the camera is quite disappointing and the battery life is not so good, while the charging speed is very high." This kind of review contains three attributes "design", "camera", and "charging speed" with complicated sentiments. As a result, most existing studies cannot handle such reviews correctly because they cannot identify the attributes and their corresponding sentiments, and will not take the hierarchical relationships of attributes into consideration for sentiment analysis. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach called Hierarchical Labeling-Sentiment Ontology Tree (HL-SOT) to label a product's attributes and their associated sentiments in product reviews by a Hierarchical Learning (HL) process with a defined Sentiment Ontology Tree (SOT). The proposed HL-SOT approach mainly includes three steps: (1) preprocessing, including tokenizing,lemmatizing and named entity recognition (NER); (2) hierarchical labeling, identifying the product attributes and their hierarchical relationships; (3) sentiment learning, predicting the sentiment of each identified attribute and its associated sentiment. The HL process is used to learn the parameters of the sentiment ontology tree by maximizing a likelihood function calculated from labeled product reviews. We also discuss how the proposed HL-SOT approach can be easily generalized to labeling a mix of reviews of more than one product. We empirically evaluate the proposed HL-SOT approach using a human-labeled dataset and report that it demonstrates promising and reasonable performance. The rest of the paper is organized as follows: we review related works on sentiment analysis and discuss their limitations in Section 2. We present the proposed HL-SOT approach in detail in Section 3. We evaluate the proposed HL-SOT approach using a human-labeled dataset and compare it to several existing studies in Section 4. Finally, we conclude this paper and discuss the future work in Section 5. Sentiment analysis has been the most studied area in the field of natural language processing (NLP) for years, and can be used in many applications, such as product quality evaluation, customer feedback analysis and opinion mining.

Throughout the years, various approaches have been proposed to tackle GEC, relying on machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques (Blue, 2002, Papineni et al., 2002). Today, researchers have put forward two state-of-the-art approaches that appear promising in this domain: machine translation (MT) and machine learning classifiers. Personalized search has been a long-standing challenge in information retrieval, with the goal of tailoring search results to individual users' preferences (Jung et al., 2017;Wang et al., 2017;Gao et al., 2019;Zhang et al., 2019). Traditionally, search personalization relies on analyzing a user's past search activities and related metadata (Chapelle and Linden, 2007;Harris and Shaban-Nejad, 2009;Yi et al., 2012). However, when a user has limited past search activities, the traditional methods based solely on past usage information face significant challenges (Lin et al., 2014). Moreover, as users tend to create, share, and discuss content through various online platforms, an increasing volume of social data (e.g., social annotations, likes, shares, comments) becomes available and can serve as a valuable resource to complement traditional usage data (Cai et al., 2010;Kim et al., 2012). Therefore, leveraging social data to enhance personalized search has attracted growing attention (Li et al., 2011;Zhang et al., 2016). In this paper, we delve into the problem of search personalization with limited past usage information, where the user profile is typically inaccurate and may not capture the user's interests effectively. We propose two probabilistic latent topic models that effectively exploit social annotations, documents, and an external knowledge base constructed from usage histories to build enhanced user profiles. This User Profile is used for topical query expansion, which expands the original query with related social annotations and web pages. To evaluate the proposed approaches, we extensively experiment on a large public social annotation dataset. Our results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed models over traditional personalized query expansion methods, which use user profiles solely built from past usage information. This consists of: (1) Enhanced User Profiles: Given that users have only limited past search activities, traditional user profiling methods may not accurately capture their interests. To address this limitation, we develop enhanced user profiles (EUPs) that combine the benefits of three different data sources: social annotations, documents, and an external knowledge base constructed from usage histories. Social annotations serve as a rich source of user feedback, providing insight into the user's interests and preferences (Kim et al., 2012). Documents capture the relationships between the user's interests and the web pages they interact with (Lin et al., 2014). Furthermore, the external knowledge base enhances the EUPs by incorporating contextual information and background knowledge about the annotated resources (Zhang et al., 2016). We present two probabilistic latent topic models, to jointly model the social annotations, documents, and the external knowledge base.

Recent advancements in neural machine translation (NMT) have led to state-of-the-art performance in various benchmarks. A widely adopted architecture in NMT nowadays is the encoder-decoder framework, which typically consists of a recurrent neural network (RNN) encoder and a sequence-to-sequence decoder. Although remarkable progress has been achieved with the encoder-decoder framework, it still has some limitations. Firstly, the RNN structure, which is inherently sequential, has difficulty in retaining distant information in long-range sequences, suppressing its ability in drawing multi-span relations across the source sentence. As a result, RNN architecture tends to forget the information that may be essential in many cases. Secondly, the traditional encoding process is focused only on one-to-one mapping from the source to the output embedding space. However, source words often have inherent relationships with each other. These inter-word relationships are rarely considered during the encoding step and if overlooked, will eventually impact the overall performance of the model. For instance, suppose we have a source sentence, which describes an entity called "Santa's little helper in reindeer wrapping, Sancho is more experienced, Rehan is struggling with the tool sorting,". If we naively conduct the encoding, the processing of each word is theoretically independent, requiring no consideration of relationships. These relationships are certain to affect the generation of translations in different sentences as they may represent genuine correlations in relationships of the words. However, the recipients of these communications may only know and understand some of the finer details. Our final goal is to develop solutions to these challenging although straightforward problems by proposing a couple of improvements to the encoding and inference components. Our main goal in this paper is to present a relation network-enhanced encoder-decoder model that addresses the issues mentioned previously. We introduce the concept of relation networks that learns the inherent relationships between source words during the encoding step, preserves the information across distant spans of the input sequence, and enhances the representations with these relationships. This relation network-equipped encoder captures the relatively long-range and soft relationships between words, engenders the encoding scheme more powerful than the basic encoderdecoder framework in memory usage, offering more adaptability in positional dependencies. In more detailed design, we integrate an additional softmax layer after the final RNN layer in the encoder as a relation classifier where the input vector is the concatenation of the encoded word sequence and its word IDs, the output vector being a set of weights for subjectivity relationships.

Neural machine translation (NMT) has become the dominant model architecture in the field of machine translation in recent years. A typical NMT system generates a translation by sampling a sequence of words from a probability distribution over the target vocabulary, conditioned on the source sentence and the decoder's internal state. 1 The probability distributions are usually obtained using a group of parallel recurrent neural networks and an attention mechanism. However, the main challenge with these systems is that they do not output a single translation, but rather sample from the probability distribution at each time step, resulting in a family of possible translations. To alleviate this issue, the concept of beam search was introduced, which aims at keeping the K most likely candidates at each time step (K is a hyperparameter known as beam size) by selecting the best next token at each step. One of the advantages of using beam search is that it modifies the sampled output distribution at each time step and can dramatically improve the quality of the translation in comparison to the greedily selected sequence. However, beam search also introduces several issues, one of which is that the selection process at each time step reduces the search space for the next step. This issue is compounded when the relevant candidate pool size, which is driven by the sum of the inverse of the probability of each candidate at each time step, is restricted. A second issue with beam search arises when the number of candidates that has been generated at any time step is greater than the size of the beam, which forces the algorithm to first select which subset of candidates to keep and then prunes the rest. While relatively inexpensive computationally, this pruning step is also another point in time where the search space has been reduced, by virtue of the reduction in the candidate pool size, and so further worsens the curse of search space amplification inherent in beam search. We will see in the next section that both of the above-mentioned pitfalls can damage the quality of the translation provided by beam search. Beam search typically accepts relatively large number of candidates, though it may discard subsets of candidates, thereby resetting the scaling factor given to the candidates. The scaling factor necessitates that the positional probabilities contributed by a candidate are scaled upwards or downwards, which can inadvertently free up extra probabilities elsewhere in the candidate pool, and hence ages the distribution unfairly by artificially shortening its tail.

Word representation learning, a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), has been extensively studied in recent years. Traditional word representations, such as word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and glove (Pennington et al., 2014), treat words as static symbols that capture their commonalities across different domains. However, words can have distinct meanings in different domains, and ignoring these domain-specific differences can lead to suboptimal performance in various NLP tasks such as text classification and sentiment analysis. Recent studies have shown that incorporating domain information into word representations can improve the performance of downstream tasks (Nguyen and Shirai, 2015;Lin et al., 2015). However, existing domain-aware word representation learning methods are largely unsupervised and often rely on an explicit identification of domain-specific word senses or label information. Furthermore, most existing methods focus on learning a single set of word representations for a given domain, without considering the potential overlap between domains. In practice, words can have multiple meanings across different domains, making it challenging to learn a single set of word representations that can capture the nuances of words in different settings. To address this challenge, we propose a novel unsupervised word representation learning method that learns domain-specific word representations for a given pair of source-target domains. Our approach is based on the idea of pivot-based learning, where we select a subset of frequent words that occur in both domains as pivots. By leveraging the co-occurrence patterns of pivots and non-pivots in both domains, we optimize an objective function that enforces two critical constraints: (a) the ability of pivots to accurately predict the co-occurring non-pivots in both domains, and (b) the similarity of word representations learnt for pivots in both domains. This ensures that our learned word representations capture the domain-specific aspects of words, while also retaining their commonalities across domains. To further facilitate domain adaptation, we propose a method to utilize the learned word representations for sentiment classification tasks. By adapting word representations to the target domain, we can effectively mitigate the shift in word meanings and improve the performance of sentiment analysis tasks. In this work, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method through a series of experiments on a benchmark dataset. We show that our approach significantly outperforms competitive baselines, including state-of-the-art domain-insensitive word representations, and achieve the best sentiment classification accuracy for all domain-pairs.

Phrases are composite units of language that contribute to the compositionality and expressiveness of natural language (Sag et al., 2002). In linguistics, the term 'phrase' typically refers to a group of two or more words that express a concept or meaning that is more abstract and complex than the meanings expressed by any of the individual group members. In machine translation and natural language processing, the use of phrases can also provide benefits such as improved fluency, idiomaticity, and overall quality of the MT output. However, phrases are not always explicitly represented in natural language processing models and are often seen as a byproduct of processing single words. Recent advances in neural machine translation (NMT) have shown remarkable progress in translating sentences, but the word-by-word encoding-decoding process of NMT finds it hard to capture the complex meanings conveyed by phrases. Sequential processing models, such as neural sequence-to-sequence models, are widely used in natural language processing, speech recognition and machine translation (Sutskever et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2014). Traditional sequential processing models require a fixed input sequence. However, when dealing with human language or speech, it is often difficult to capture uncertainty and variability in the input sequence. For example, in speech recognition, one input sequence may have multiple possible transcript representations due to ambiguity or uncertainty in the acoustic signals. In machine translation, a single sentence may have multiple possible parses due to varying part-of-speech tagging or semantics. The input to the neural model is usually determined by an up-stream system, such as a word segmenter, part of speech tagger, or speech recognizer. However, these up-stream models may themselves be error-prone. Incorporating uncertainty at the input level can benefit the neural model by capturing the ambiguity and variability in the data, but does require additional memory and processing, which affects computational efficiency. One common way to represent uncertain inputs in a compact form is to use word lattices, which capture the possible words or word sequences and their posterior probabilities in a compact, yet flexible, structure. Word lattices have been used in previous work for incorporating uncertainty into some models (Sainath et al., 2015), but have so far not been used with efficient neural LSTMs (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997). We introduce a neural lattice-to-sequence model that can consume word lattices and incorporate their posterior scores in a computationally efficient way. Building on the TreeLSTM (Tai et al., 2015), we extend the childsum and forget gates to account for multiple possible sequences and their weights, and introduce an additional bias in the attention mechanism to propagate the lattice scores. This consists of two main components: (1) incorporating lattice scores into the TreeLSTM architecture and (2) adapting the encoder part of an attentional sequence-to-sequence model to process word lattices. This adaptation necessitates modification of the internal workings of a careful design, specifically the attention mechanism within the encoder-decoder model. In our architecture, we maintain and integrate posterior scores of a lattice as well as 'regular' outputs of this lattice. Our implementation leverages attention mechanism for increased parallelization. Our method captures uncertainty and distribution of possible inputs naturally by representing input as a set of possible word or sequence outputs and their associated probabilities, which allows us to estimate the quality of output sequences more precisely.

Topic modeling is a prominent research direction that aims to automatically extract a set of abstract topics from a large-scale unstructured text corpus. In recent years, topic modeling has been widely applied in various areas, including text mining, information retrieval, sentiment analysis, opinion mining and document summarization. Due to its importance and practicality, numerous topic modeling techniques have been developed and successfully applied in various applications. However, most topic modeling techniques aim to discover the underlying semantic topics of a large-scale text corpus as a whole, ignoring the diversity and variability within each topic. The existing research [Li et al., 2018;Xu and Hong, 2016] indicates that there often exist significant intra-topic variability in natural language datasets, which significantly degrade the performance of downstream tasks such as topic classification and sentiment analysis. The key problem is that these existing topic modeling techniques fail to explicitly capture intra-topic variability, leading to distorted semantic representation and inferior classification results. This lack of understanding of intra-topic variability and its impact on downstream tasks motivates further research to advance this direction. Variances in document style, vocabulary usage, and syntactic structures can all contribute to the intra-topic variability issue, as shown in relevant research [Zhang and Banerjee, 2017;D TomozeiandA CeffRevPTjasiene, 2014]. Specifically, topic modeling techniques that fail to normalize the intra-topic variability may produce distorted topic features, such that documents expressing differing viewpoints on the same topic fall under the same topic category [Wang andMcCallum, 2017]. To tackle this challenge, there are mainly three methods used in recent years: i) Data augmentation [Miao et al., 2008] that artificially generate new synthesized intra-topic samples to normalize intra-topic variability; ii)Model regularization [Zhu et al., 2018] that incorporate the low-level variability into the optimization objective to suppress intra-topic variations; and iii)Feature normalization [Xia et al., 2014] that transforms the topic features so that it can suppress intra-topic variations. To improve these methods, we raise two considerations. Firstly, we expect that the topic representation should alleviate intra-topic variability without making unrealistic assumptions about the distribution of document features. In other words, it is meaningful that the topic representation can normalize intra-topic variability without apriori knowledge about the data distribution that the topic model needs to satisfy the distribution properties( e.g., the principal axes of zero mean and unit variance). Secondly, the intra-topic variability normalization method does not need any additional data or computational complexity.

Most work has focused on either count-based n-gram models or sophisticated neural networks. Word segmentation is a critical preprocessing step for many NLP tasks, including statistical machine translation (SMT). In languages that do not have explicit word delimiters, like Chinese and Japanese, word segmentation is particularly challenging. Usually, a word segmentation (WS) scheme is selected based on the purpose of the NLP task and the available training data.
