Machine translation is a challenging task that involves translating content from one language (source language) into another language (target language). Traditional machine translation systems are trained on a specific source-target language pair and have limited ability to adapt to new languages or domains. With the increasing availability of large-scale multilingual data and the development of deep learning techniques, there has been a growing interest in developing methods for multi-source and multi-target machine translation (Arivazhagan et al., 2019;Fan et al., 2019;Miculicich et al., 2018;Wong et al., 2019). Multi-source machine translation involves translating from multiple source languages into a target language, where each source language may have its own translation history or linguistic features that are different from one another (Fan et al., 2019). On the other hand, multi-target machine translation involves translating from a single source language into multiple target languages, where each target language may have its own linguistic features, syntax, or semantics that are different from one another. In this paper, we propose a method for multi-target machine translation, where the goal is to perform simultaneous translation from a single source language to multiple target languages. The motivation behind our proposed approach is that information about multiple target languages can be useful for improving the translation quality of the source language, especially when there are strong linguistic relationships between the languages. There are several scenarios where our approach is useful: (1) When only a weak language model is available for a target language. In these cases, the quality of the translations can be improved by leveraging the knowledge from a strong language model of a related target language. (2) When there are multiple related target languages. The modeling of the linguistic relationships between these languages can provide valuable information that is useful for translation. (3) When there is a limited amount of training data available for the target languages. In this case, learning from a related but larger language model can help improve the translation quality. In the following, we provide a detailed description of our proposed multi-target machine translation framework, which is based on the formalism of synchronous context-free grammars. This framework is specifically designed to handle multiple target languages and is free from the limitations of traditional machine translation approaches. Synchronous context-free grammars are a type of formal grammar that can handle multiple input and output languages at the same time (Alshawi, 1992).

Demographic attributes such as age and gender are abundant unobserved variables in text data generated from social media. They are valuable for multiple applications such as personalization, product recommendation, user profiling, and more. Despite their importance, there is a lack of robust and accurate tools that can infer demographic attributes directly from text data. We propose an approach to develop predictive lexica, which can be used to indirectly infer demographic attributes from text data. Lexical analysis has been a potential tool for demographic inference, with words and their distribution varying by age and gender. The success of lexical inference relies on the development of robust predictive lexica that capture the co-variate of words (containing age and genderrelated information) with demographic attributes. A range of studies have shown word usage to be influenced by age (Schacter and Pelham, 1989;Holtgraves, 2002;Bolender, 2011), with results that cohere with Grieve, Mahar, and Sibley (2009). Moreover, certain words tend to be associated with specific age groups, e.g. 60, heyday for the older individuals. The issue is highly linguistic and relevant for various tasks, especially for population demographic studies, business market segmentation and recommendation systems. Furthermore, another key aspect of demographic inference is the distinction between different demographic groups, which is classically known as the gender classification. In recent years, considerable research focus has seen, and indeed some success has been registered by the integration of machine learning algorithms to extract insights about the gender of the person posting content online (Eyvindarson, 2004;Heikkilä & Isotalo, 2001), where supervised modeling enables identification of the specific linguistic cues in the text and how these correspond to gender (Grieve, Cook Walters, & Marsh, 2010) This demonstrates that development of well specified elderly prediction predictors can enable identification of female writers and lead to an understanding of gender and age demographics of social media users. In this paper, we outline an approach to develop lexica for demographic attributes from text data. We use regression and classification models from a dataset consisting of word usage in Facebook, blog, and Twitter data with associated demographic labels to derive predictive lexica ages and gender. The lexica offered publicly reach a state of the art in age and gender inference in several benchmarks and demonstrate the potential of our approach by the distribution of words in different fractions on social media profiles and based on diverse sourced corpora. Our approach is, therefore, designto enable inference of age and gender attributes from large-scale social media distributions using low-regret text and regression models in predictive lexica following the demand for scalable, widely available solutions.

Zero-shot learning (ZSL) has emerged as a promising area of research in computer vision, natural language processing, and other domains (Lampert et al., 2009;Tommasi et al., 2013). The idea is to learn models that can generalize from a limited set of seen classes to an unlimited set of unseen classes (Lampert et al., 2009). ZSL approaches typically rely on learning a mapping between the feature space and a semantic space (Li et al., 2010). The semantic space is often constructed by inducing a word embedding space from corpus data (Xu et al., 2016). Zero-shot classification is then performed by mapping an input representation from the feature space to a point in the word embedding space, selecting the closest word(s) to the mapped point as candidate class labels (Larochelle et al., 2012). A key challenge in ZSL is the establishment of an effective mapping between the feature and semantic spaces. This is typically achieved through deep neural models that project the input representations from the feature space to the semantic space (Kodirov et al., 2013). However, the current performance of cross-space mapping methods is still quite low, resulting in poor generalization abilities (Chen et al., 2016). In this paper, we focus on the analysis and improvement of cross-space mapping methods. In particular, we shed light on the properties of cross-space mapping functions that relate to the concept of hubness (Diehl et al., 2018) and pollution (Krichene et al., 2017). Hubness corresponds to the phenomenon where a few high-dimensional points have many close neighbors, which can cause issues in mapping similarity calculations in the semantic space (Diehl et al., 2018). Pollution, on the other hand, refers to the presence of noisy or irrelevant labels in the training data (Krichene et al., 2017). Our analysis reveals that hubness and pollution have significant effects on the performance of cross-space mapping functions. We develop approaches to mitigate these issues by adaptively normalizing the feature representations and selecting robust word embeddings. These methods are validated through extensive experimentation on benchmark ZSL datasets, yielding significant improvements over state of the art results. Additionally, we evaluate our approaches in the context of cross-linguistic (English-Frenchword translation) and cross-modal (object categorization in images) applications. Our work contributes to a better understanding of the properties of cross-space mapping functions and enables the construction of more effective ZSL models. The improved performance of our methods facilitates the efficient adaptation to novel and unseen classes in real-world applications.

Multi-document summarization is a challenging task that deals with generating a concise summary from a large collection of documents. A key challenge in this task is to effectively rank and select the most relevant sentences that accurately capture the main information in the source documents. A closely related and fundamental challenge is query-focused summarization, which requires the system to focus on the specific information relevant to a particular query. This task is ideal for use cases such as Information Retrieval (IR) systems, where providing users with a concise summary of the relevant information is crucial to save their valuable time. The demand for succinct yet informative summaries has motivated the development of various data-driven summarization methods that aim to identify the most relevant information to include in the summary. Recent advances have shown that using the linguistic structure of the text can be extremely beneficial for recognizing key information and highlighting the essential meanings (Gillick et al., 2009). Previous work on multi-document and query-focused summarization has mainly relied on superficial cues, such as bag-of-words, which neglects more structured information. For example, in short document summarization, the Relative Position Analysis (RPA) framework identified that a sentence's position is highly correlated with relevant information(Gerber and Chambers, 2015), but RPA is not considered in current deep multi-document summarization models. In order to improve these summarization methods, we need a more structured approach that is able to represent the text at a finer-grained level, accounting for the finer details of the text while providing an accurate and informative summary.( although there are models based on neural networks but still the major shortcoming is lack of robust linguistic representation for improving summarization). To address this challenge, recent studies have proposed modeling the sentence as a structured representation by using parsing trees and exploiting their syntactic and semantic properties to form a better understanding of the sentence's content ( dosa-Santana et al., 2017). Restricting ourselves to structured representations has an additional advantage that there's increased efficiency in recognizing redundant content in subsets of sentences, thereby forming the key factor for choosing sentence compression as our baseline. Our work makes two main contributions. Firstly we take a more structured approach to query-focused multi-document summarization by leveraging the parse trees to filter and select relevant sentences. Our model achieves superior performance than previous state-of-art models on several metrics such as ROUGE (Lin, 2004).

Preposition error correction is a crucial task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), given the pervasive presence of preposition errors in written text, particularly in student writing, and the difficulty of correcting them automatically (Felbaum et al., 2004). Current statistical models for preposition error correction are typically trained and evaluated on a specific test set, although they are expected to generalize to other, unseen test sets (Brannon and Mayfield, 2001;Hovy and Lin, 1999;Sakoe and Chiba, 1988). However, these models often fail to generalize across very different test sets (Lai et al., 2015). For instance, a system trained using well-edited text is unlikely to perform well when tested on noisy, unedited text (Felbaum et al., 2004). We argue that this lack of generalizability is due to the use of either well-edited text or error-annotated corpora, which tend to be biased towards specific error characteristics (Brannon and Mayfield, 2001). Consequently, we propose to train preposition error correction systems using a more robust and diverse corpus, extracted from Wikipedia revisions. This new, large corpus is designed to capture the complexities of preposition errors and their corrections, and is expected to facilitate the development of more generalizable systems. We motivate our approach by highlighting the limitations of existing methods and the importance of robust preposition error correction in NLP applications. We begin by discussing the prevalence of preposition errors and the importance of correcting them (Felbaum et al., 2004), as well as the limitations of current statistical models for preposition error correction (Lai et al., 2015). We then introduce our new, large error-annotated corpus, automatically extracted from Wikipedia revisions, and highlight its characteristics and advantages over existing corpora (Felbaum et al., 2004;Brannon and Mayfield, 2001). Finally, we present the results of our experiments, in which we train preposition error correction systems using our new corpus and evaluate their performance on three different test sets, each from a different domain and with different error characteristics (Felbaum et al., 2004). Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in developing more robust preposition error correction systems that generalize across very different test sets. The need for robust preposition error correction arises from the pervasive presence of preposition errors in written text (Felbaum et al., 2004). These errors can have significant consequences, particularly in academic, professional, and technical writing (Brannon and Mayfield, 2001). For instance, incorrect prepositions can completely change the meaning of a sentence, leading to confusion and misunderstandings (Felbaum et al., 2004).

Traditional machine translation systems have been widely used for decades due to their high performance on many tasks. However, these systems often rely on multiple techniques and heavy feature engineering, and the parameters are hard to be tuned. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in developing end-to-end learning architectures for machine translation, particularly those based on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and their variants, such as long short-term memory (LSTM) networks and gated recurrent units (GRUs). Unlike traditional systems, Neural Machine Translation (NMT) systems learn the parameters of the model and require minimal preprocessing, which greatly reduce the manual data preprocessing steps. However, the end-to-end learning paradigm also comes with new challenges, one of which is the out-of-vocabulary (OOV) problem. The OOV problem occurs when the source or target side word is not seen during training, and the model cannot generate or recognize the word correctly due to the fixed input or output word size. In practice, memory and time constraints typically require NMT systems to only take a fixed number of words into account, which is 4,096 to 16,384 in the current transformer-based models, giving rise to the OOV problem. In German, word order is relatively free, which often leads to longer sentences and more frequent out-of-vocabulary events compared to English. We identify two main reasons for the OOV problem in NMT: firstly, German compound words, such as `Schuldbuch` (debt book), whose solutions are much harder although straightforward. They are composed of two or three written words and are even harder than agglutinative compounds. Secondly, but also a main challenge for indic roots, German base words almost never change when conjugated and are much larger than in English: this forces to form either an inflexibly massive testing set (treat the low-estimate consists of rare words only ) or extremely limited support for compounds. In an attempt to alleviate the OOV problem, we analyze the effectiveness of using compound word splitters for the source side German texts in this paper. Specifically, we implement two different preprocessing techniques: a) using the word-splitting approach to break up German compound words, and b) inserting separator tokens to indicate where to split a compound word. We experiment with both approaches on the WMT'14 German-to-English translation task, showing a +2.5 BLEU points improvement over the baseline on the development set.

Machine translation is a challenging task that involves translating content from one language to another. Significant improvements have been achieved with the advent of deep learning techniques, particularly neural machine translation (NMT) approaches. However, NMT models are typically single-decoder systems that produce one final translation per input sentence. In the context of machine translation, it is well known that using multiple translations, rather than a single translation, can significantly improve translation quality (Zhang et al., 2005; Och and Ney, 2003). This is because different translation systems will have different strengths and weaknesses, and a single-decoder system can only capture the strengths of that particular system (Galley et al., 2006). System combination and Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) decoding are two commonly used approaches to combine the outputs of multiple machine translation decoders (Chen et al., 2014;Xu et al., 2013). These approaches first compute an n-best list or word lattice from multiple decoders, and then postprocess the list by scoring each translation based on its compatibility with the outputs from other decoders. However, these approaches have two main drawbacks. Firstly, they sometimes result in "over-correction" of translation errors, as the system may over-weight the opinions of the weaker decoders (Zhang et al., 2010). Secondly, they require a potentially large amount of additional computation to postprocess the n-best lists, which can offset the benefits of using multiple decoders. We propose a new approach that combines the strengths of multiple machine translation decoders in real-time, without the need for postprocessing. This new approach is called collaborative decoding, or co-decoding for short. In co-decoding, we use an iterative decoding approach where each decoder explores a set of partial hypotheses in parallel, and exchanges these partial translations with other decoders. We then compute translation consensus metrics, such as n-gram agreement statistics, between the partial translations from multiple decoders. These consensus metrics are used to re-rank both the full and partial hypotheses explored by the decoders, effectively allowing them to influence each other within the decoding process. This has two key benefits. Firstly, it allows the decoders to correct each other's mistakes and blend their strengths in a more dynamic way than traditional system combination and MBR decoding. Secondly, the re-ranking process only requires a relatively small amount of additional computation, as the decoders are evaluating the same set of partial hypotheses that they already explored in decoding.

The importance of news and information cannot be overstated in the realm of finance. News events have the ability to shift the intrinsic value of companies instantaneously. There are numerous prior studies which have demonstrated that news can affect stock prices (Baker and Wurgler, 2013), and the impact of news on financial markets is substantial (Lennox and Zhang, 2013). However, current methods for extracting valuable information from news are typically limited in their potential. Prior research in finance often relies on traditional methods such as textual sentiment analysis (Bayer et al., 2016) to capture the information content of news. However, many of the existing models have several shortcomings. Firstly, they only consider one specific feature which is sentiment. The sentiment features are often found to be extremely limiting because of the complexity of financial news. News reports may discuss both positive and negative sentiment aspects simultaneously and if only one is taken into account, the co-existence of these conflicting sentiment aspects can either cancel out each other which affects the overall efficiency of the model or shift in priorities such that the effect of any particular positive or negative sentiment is overlooked. Moreover, the current methods fail to consider factors relevant to the field, such as specific news articles, events, or companies. A major limitation to traditional sentiment analysis of news is its lack of abstraction: sentences can have complex structures and ambiguities, potentially resulting in misidentification of the recipients' attitude (preference, sentiment, emotion) (Yin et al., 2009). Therefore, there is a significant need for better tools and techniques for analyzing the information content of news text. The goal of this paper is to present a novel approach by leveraging recent breakthroughs in deep learning that go beyond traditional sentiment analysis. With the emergence of e-commerce and consumer platforms, the availability of user-generated reviews has become a valuable resource for customers to make informed purchasing decisions. In this context, product review analysis has become a crucial task, with consumer reviews serving as an essential source of information to assess product qualities and characteristics. Opinion questions about product aspects are common, allowing users to seek detailed information on features and attributes, making informed purchasing decisions easier and faster. However, due to the sheer volume of potential product aspects, as well as their increasing complexity, simply searching for keyword matching is not sufficient to answer such opinion questions. Consumer reviews contain rich information enabling retrieval of relevant answers to many of the questions asked by customers, but to effectively leverage this information, it is necessary to first properly identify the product aspects referred to in the questions and the opinions on these aspects expressed by other consumers. The conventional method of retrieving answers to opinion questions relies on simple keyword matching and search in the review text. However, it is well-known that this basic method typically produces results of poor quality, mainly because it fails to take into account the context, the organization and the underlying hierarchy of the product aspects that are the focus of the questions. As relevant review fragments often contain other words besides keywords, thus involving synonyms or even multiple keywords, these conventional methods are certain to be insensitive to the nuances in different sentences as well as overlook relationships between different aspects mentioned in reviews. In this paper, we develop a new framework, called HAQA (Hierarchical Aspect Question Answering), which can quickly and effectively retrieve the answers to opinion questions based on the exploitation of the organization, such as the parentchild relationships in the hierarchical structures inherent to product aspects mentioned in consumer reviews. Through HAQA, we can identify the specific product aspects in the question and pinpoint their sub-aspects without going through any preceding statements, and determine whether these sub-aspects manifest themselves as explicitly stated in the review text or are implicit and implied in the context. In turn, we can gather the corresponding fragment reviews relative to product aspects to provide readers, thereby generating the exact responses given their questions. A crucial factor in determining the effectiveness of our proposed approach is a careful consideration of four critical criteria, which can provide respondents with answers that are both meaningful to the specific aspect of a product of interest and meaningful in the particular context of the question posed to the responder.

Generating concise and accurate highlights from a news article is an essential task in summarization. However, automatically producing news highlights is very challenging, mainly due to the long length and complexity of news articles. Current summarization methods rely heavily on machine learning-based approaches, which often require large amounts of annotated data and computational resources. Furthermore, these methods may struggle to capture the essence and nuance of a news story. Recent years have seen a proliferation of microblogs, such as Twitter, providing an immense wealth of user-generated content in the form of short, informative posts. The microblogging platform has a unique characteristic – the artificial compression effect due to the character limit of the posts. This limit essentially forces users to distill their thoughts into concise, actionable, and highly relevant information. As such, microblog posts often inherently possess an "essentialist" property that captures the essence of a news story. In many cases, microbloggers would share quotes or excerpts of news articles in their own words, either to spark a discussion or comment on the news piece. These microblog posts not only provide valuable signals of important pieces of information in the news story but also amplify the dissemination of news across online communities. In this work, we propose a novel approach to improve news highlights extraction using microblogs. By leveraging the benefits of microblogs, we hypothesize that these can serve as effective supplements to traditional text summarization methods. In particular, we seek to capitalize on the inherently concise and informative nature of microblog posts as a noise-tolerant and scalable resource for automating the extraction of news highlights. Given a news article and a corresponding set of microblog posts, our method consists of two rank-then-extract tasks. First, we use a tweet-violator-score-based (TVS) ranking algorithm to identify a subset of microblog posts that are most indicative of the news story's essence. These indicative microblog posts will then be used to assist in the ranking of news sentences for extraction. The goal is to leverage the microblog posts to provide context, thereby augmenting the accuracy of sentence extraction. Second, we present a reverse ranking (RR) approach that treats the microblog posts as an additional source of sentences for extraction. Instead of relying on traditional ranking methods, we rank the microblog posts based on their similarity to a set of seed microblog posts, and then select several top-ranked microblog posts as substitutes for news sentences.

Generating expository dialogue from monologue is a task that has garnered significant attention in recent years within the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community. Expository dialogue, which conveys information while depicting a conversation, has been recognized as a powerful tool for presenting complex ideas, beliefs, and knowledge in an engaging and accessible manner. In educational settings, group discussions, and online communication, expository dialogue plays a crucial role in facilitating understanding and stimulating critical thinking. Moreover, the potential applications of generating expository dialogue from monologue are vast, encompassing fields such as education, marketing, and language translation. By automating the process of converting monologues into engaging dialogues, we can effectively enhance the dissemination of information, increase user engagement, and facilitate the development of more sophisticated language models. However, generating expository dialogue from monologue remains a challenging task due to the inherent differences between the two forms of discourse. Monologues are typically composed of continuous streams of narrative or expository text, whereas dialogues typically involve a sequence of turns between multiple speakers, each contributing to the conversation through their own turn of speech. These differences make it essential to address the following questions: What does it mean to "convert" a monologue into a dialogue? What information or properties should be preserved in this transformation process? How can we represent the underlying structure of conversations to facilitate the generation of high-quality expository dialogue? Answering these questions will not only help us develop effective methods for generating expository dialogue but also shed light on the complex interactions between speakers and the communicative mechanisms that govern human conversation. To address the challenge of generating expository dialogue from monologue, we require high-quality training data that accurately represents the properties of both monologues and dialogues. Toward this end, we have compiled a parallel corpus of monologues and dialogues in English, consisting of over 10,000 paired examples of expository text and dialogue. This corpus offers a diverse range of topics, from technical explanations and educational lectures to informative product descriptions and persuasive pitches. Our corpus is not only significantly larger than existing resources but also more evenly balanced between monologues and dialogues, making it an ideal foundation for exploring the relationships between these two forms of discourse. To facilitate the development of effective methods for generating expository dialogue from monologue, we are also implementing a semi-automatic system for constructing Monologue-to-Dialogue (M2D) generation rules. By leveraging large-scale language models and pre-trained sequence-to-sequence frameworks, we can rapidly generate candidate dialogues from a given monologue, rapidly evaluate their coherence and relevance, and progressively refine the underlying generation rules to reflect the structure and semantics

Sentence simplification is a crucial NLP task where the goal is to rewrite a given complex sentence into a simpler form that preserves its original meaning. Considerable attention has been given to sentence simplification in recent years due to its importance in various applications such as language learning, text summarization, and accessibility (Raymond and Lerman, 1995; Knipp et al., 2002). Most sentence simplification approaches aim to reduce the dependency length, unpack sophisticated sentences, and make language more comprehensible (Gao et al., 2014;Yasunaga et al., 2017). Many methods use data-driven techniques based on machine translation (MT), where a sentence is simplified using an MT model trained on a parallel corpus of complex and simple sentences (Aknow and Coco, 2015). However, these approaches often struggle with small training datasets and lack the ability to perform splitting, dropping, and reordering operations that are typical in complex sentences (Weinberger et al., 2009). Moreover, traditional statistical machine translation approaches focus on short-phrase translation, which is not well-suited to the task of sentence simplification. Another major challenge in sentence simplification is how to effectively preserve the meaning of the simplified sentence while reducing its complexity. Furthermore, traditional chunking-based approaches, such as part-of-speech (POS) tagging and shallow parsing, are also not effective in sentence simplification. Even though such methods can identify some grammatical structure, they fall short in handling more complex sentence structures such as sentences with subordinate clauses (Manning and Scheffler, 1999). Moreover, as the complexity of the input sentence grows, it is increasingly difficult for these approaches to preserve the original meaning of the sentence. As a result, a more effective approach is needed that can model the transformations of complex sentences into simpler ones while preserving their meaning. In the following, we will introduce a novel model architecture for sentence simplification that is more proficient in handling the complexities of complex sentences, including splitting, dropping, reordering, and substitution. We will present our Tree-based Simplification Model and provide an efficient method to train our model using large-scale parallel datasets. In order to effectively preserve the original meaning of the input sentence while reducing its complexity, we propose a novel model architecture that explores a constituency-based approach to simplify complex sentences. Our proposed model takes as input a complex sentence and produces a simplified sentence as output. The input complex sentence is first parsed based on a Context Free Grammar (CFG) in this approach, where a parse tree is used to represent the grammatical structure of the sentence.

Relation extraction is a critical task in natural language processing (NLP), with applications in information extraction, question answering, and text summarization. The majority of existing approaches to relation extraction are based on supervised learning, where a model is trained on a hand-labeled dataset to recognize patterns and extract relationships between entities in text. However, supervised learning suffers from several major limitations. Firstly, obtaining high-quality labeled training data for relation extraction is extremely time-consuming and expensive, particularly for a large number of relation types. Furthermore, such methods are typically domain-dependent, requiring extensive adaptation to new domains or languages. Finally, the size of the labeled data is often limited, which can lead to underfitting or overfitting of the model. To address these challenges, we explore an alternative paradigm for relation extraction that eschews the need for labeled training data. By leveraging distant supervision from large, unlabeled corpora, our proposed method can automatically identify entities and extract relationships without requiring domain-specific knowledge or extensive annotation. Our approach, which we term 'distant supervision for relation extraction without labeled data,' builds on the following intuition: given a pair of entities identified in a large database, such as Freebase (Bollacker et al., 2008), the textual contexts in which these entities co-occur in a large, unlabeled corpus may provide a useful signal for inferring relationships between them. There are several key challenges to addressing this problem: (1) Information extraction (IE) is a first step which may introduce noise to extracted relations.(2) User feedback is relatively inexpensive but still too expensive and time-consuming to do on a large scale.(3) Productivity of annotators is typically high on class label that almost uniquely is determined by a few distinguishable features but much lower on multi-choice classification due either to inability to determine these few relevant features or unwillingness to guess the most likely class label when you're not 100% certain. Recently, researchers have begun exploring the use of external knowledge sources, such as lexical resources, ontologies, and semantic databases, as a means of providing distant supervision for relation extraction (Gurevych and Meyers, 2002;Swani et al., 2011). By leveraging these resources, it may be feasible to develop robust relation extraction systems that can operate with minimal supervision. One promising approach in this vein is that of utilizing large semantic databases, such as DBpedia (Bizer et al., 2009) or Freebase (Bollacker et al., 2008), which contain a large number of explicitly annotated relationships between entities.

The domain of semantic parsing has been a long-standing problem in the natural language processing (NLP) community. A key challenge in semantic parsing is the need to model the meaning of sentences while accounting for lexical variation and compositionality. Traditional approaches to semantic parsing have relied on large, hand-constructed lexicons that pair words and phrases with their syntactic and semantic content. However, such lexicons can be inefficient and inflexible when words appear repeatedly with closely related lexical content. A more flexible and generalizable approach to lexical modeling is needed to capture the nuances of language and support accurate semantic parsing. In this work, we take a data-driven approach to learning factored probabilistic Combinatory Categorical Grammar (CCG) grammars for semantic parsing. The key idea is to use factored lexicons that include both lexemes to model word meanings and templates to model systematic variation in word usage. Factored lexicons have two key advantages over traditional lexicons. First, they enable the model to learn more general, abstract representations of word meanings, which can be applied in a wider range of contexts. This reduces the need for large, hand-constructed lexicons and enables the model to learn more efficiently from data. Second, factored lexicons provide a more principled way of modeling systematic variation in word usage, which is often not well-captured in traditional lexicons. For example, a factored lexicon might include a lexeme for the word "walk" with the meaning "to move on foot", and a template to indicate that the same word can also be used in the sense of "to take a casual stroll". The template can be parameterized to capture the different nuances of word usage, such as the addition of adverbs or prepositional phrases. To learn factored CCG lexicons, we develop an algorithm that combines ideas from discrete latent variable models and low-rank matrix factorization. The algorithm takes as input a training dataset of sentences paired with logical-form meaning representations, and outputs a factored CCG lexicon, along with a probabilistic parse-selection model. The parse-selection model is responsible for selecting the most appropriate parse for a given sentence, given its lexical and syntactic context. We evaluate the performance of our approach on benchmark datasets for semantic parsing, and demonstrate that the factored CCG lexicons lead to significant improvements in generalization performance over traditional CCG lexicons. Our results show that the factored lexical model enables the parser to learn more abstract, generalizable representations of word meanings, and to capture systematic variation in word usage more effectively.

Code generation is a challenging task that has far-reaching applications in a variety of domains. This is especially true for programming languages, where the ability to generate code programmatically and efficiently is crucial for many software engineering tasks. With the increasing complexity of modern software systems, there is a growing need to develop methods for generating code automatically from high-level abstractions, specifications, or other forms of input. Recent advances in deep learning and natural language processing (NLP) have led to a proliferation of methods for generating text from various types of input, including structured and unstructured data. However, most existing approaches are designed to handle only single-input data types, such as text or images. Consequently, there is a pressing need for new architectures that can handle multiple, heterogeneous input types, such as natural language and structured data. One key challenge in designing code generation models is the need to balance the trade-off between conditioning on the input data and generating novel code. A model that conditions too strongly on the input data is unlikely to generalize well to unseen inputs, whereas a model that conditions too weakly may lose valuable information and context from the input, leading to suboptimal code generation results. Furthermore, most current methods for code generation, especially for languages with complex grammar and syntax such as programming languages, focus on character-level or token-level prediction only. These methods struggle with generating code at a higher level of abstraction, such as functions, classes, or even program structures. In addition, as software systems become ever more complex, it is becoming increasingly difficult to design and maintain code generation systems that can handle increasingly complex programming languages. Recent research has shown that code generation can significantly benefit from incorporating high-level program abstractions into the generative model. High-level representations such as program structure, data flow, and control flow graphs can provide valuable semantic information that can improve the quality and correctness of generated code. This work aims to address the challenges of code generation by presenting a novel neural network architecture that can generate an output sequence conditioned on an arbitrary number of input functions. In our approach, we represent the input data as a collection of predictor functions, each of which can depend on the output from previous predictors. This allows the model to learn a hierarchical representation of the input data that captures relationships between different aspects of the code.

Question Answering over Knowledge Bases (KB-QA) has become one of the most important natural language processing (NLP) tasks, which nowadays see applications in many areas, such as artificial intelligence (AI) assistants, recommendation systems, and databases. The general goal of KB-QA is to directly answer user questions based on the facts stored in a Knnowledge Base (KB). This task gained significant attention with the release of the open-domain question answering task of the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD) (Rajpurkar et al., 2016;Wang et al., 2017). SQuAD test contains many question answering (Q&A) pairs that refer to a context, where the context is a small part of a long passage from Wikipedia. Solving this task involves a type of KB-QA with predefined contextual information. Extending KB-QA to the entire Wikipedia or a larger corpus remains a challenge due to the ever-growing size of the KB and the need for large-scale QA systems that can scale up to a global document universe. Simple questions are the most common type of questions in web queries. The great ease of use of search engines like Google and Bing has made them essential tools in humans' daily information seeking behavior. A major design goal is to handle the intrinsic complexity of natural language questions in a manner that keeps users from being required to anticipate the formal representation of facts for search. Even simple questions seen in web queries often comprise prerequisite language skills such as entity recognition and complex factual knowledge such that end users may not possess. Discourse relations in natural language have been studied for several decades, and regardless of the application domain, such as argumentation mining (Stab et al., 2012), text summarization (Yoshida et al., 2014), conversation (Higashinaka et al., 2014), question answering (Verberne et al., 2007), information extraction (Cimiano et al., 2005) and opinion mining (Lei et al., 2015) the identification of certain relationships between different parts of text, called discourse relations, is a crucial part of the Natural Language Processing (NLP) pipeline. These relationships help human readers to infer meaningful connections between different parts of the text. However, discourse relations can be extremely challenging to identify because of their complex and subtle nature. In general, discourse relations can be broadly categorized into explicit and implicit relations (Prasad et al., 2008), as illustrated in the following example: 2 The company was disappointed by the ruling. because The obligation is totally unwarranted. (adapted from wsj 0294) The explicit relation identified in the preceding sentence is an instance of causal relation triggered by the trigger word 'because.' notwithstanding, the preceding example illustrates an implicit relation. Implicit discourse relations are inherently more difficult to identify as they lack clear explicit markers, as opposed to explicit relations. There are around 48 possible types of implicit discourse relations seen in the PDTB (Prasad et al., 2008). However, state-of-the-art systems have found it challenging to model these complex relationships, and this is also echoed in the significantly lower performance scores for this task compared to those of explicit relation identification. In addition, almost half of the data in the PDTB falls under the implicit discourse relation category (Sporleder and Lascarides, 2008). That being the case, improving the performance of implicit discourse relation identification is an important area of research within the realm of NLP.
